name: Football (Soccer)
visual_anchor: Dynamic low-angle slow-motion shot of a classic black-and-white patterned ball ripping into the top corner netting under bright stadium floodlights.
core_traits: Played by two opposing teams of eleven players on a rectangular grass pitch
Outfield players cannot touch the spherical ball with their hands or arms during play
Features ninety minutes of regulation time split into two equal halves
Goalkeepers are the only players permitted to handle the ball within the penalty box

facts_and_myths.claim: The word soccer was originally coined in England, not the United States.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The term originated as Oxford slang shortening 'Association Football' in the late nineteenth century before American adoption.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The FIFA World Cup final is watched by over one billion people worldwide.

facts_and_myths.claim: Referees have always used yellow and red cards since the first international matches.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Penalty cards were introduced at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico, inspired by British referee Ken Aston's observation of traffic lights.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Before penalty cards, referees had to verbally communicate cautions in noisy multi-language stadiums.

name: Basketball
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical closeup of an orange pebbled leather ball swishing through a suspended white nylon net attached to a glowing plexiglass backboard.
core_traits: Played on a hardwood court with five players per side competing to score through an elevated hoop
Players advance the ball by bouncing it while running or passing to teammates
Scoring yields two or three points depending on distance from the target hoop
Features a shot clock that forces offensive teams to attempt a shot within a fixed window

facts_and_myths.claim: The earliest basketball games were played using peach baskets and a soccer ball.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dr. James Naismith nailed two peach baskets to gymnasium balcony railings in Springfield, Massachusetts in 1891.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Someone had to manually retrieve the ball from the basket with a ladder after every point until bottoms were cut out.

facts_and_myths.claim: The three-point line has existed since the very creation of professional basketball.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The NBA did not adopt the three-point line until the 1979-1980 season, testing it after the rival ABA league popularized it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chris Ford scored the first NBA three-pointer on October 12, 1979.

name: Tennis
visual_anchor: High-speed vertical shot of a bright optic-yellow fuzzy ball compressing against woven racket strings amidst kicked-up red clay dust.
core_traits: Racket sport played individually or in doubles across a low net on grass, clay, or hard surfaces
Unique point scoring system progressing through 15, 30, 40, and game
Matches are structured into sets where players must win at least six games by a margin of two
Server gets two chances to deliver the ball diagonally into the opponent's service box

facts_and_myths.claim: Tennis balls were originally white or black before fluorescent yellow was adopted.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Optic yellow balls were introduced in 1972 after television research proved they were easier for home viewers to track on screen.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Wimbledon maintained traditional white tennis balls until 1986.

facts_and_myths.claim: The tennis term 'love' for zero points comes from an English phrase meaning playing for passion.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Most etymologists trace 'love' to the French word 'l'oeuf' meaning egg, representing the zero shape on a scoreboard.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A game tied at 40-40 is called deuce, derived from the French 'deux' meaning two consecutive points needed.

name: Swimming
visual_anchor: Crystal-clear underwater vertical camera tracking a swimmer cutting through turquoise chlorinated water leaving a shimmering trail of air bubbles.
core_traits: Aquatic racing discipline contested across standard 50-meter Olympic-sized pools
Features four primary competitive strokes: freestyle, backstroke, breaststroke, and butterfly
Athletes launch off elevated starting blocks and execute tumble turns against the wall
Events range from explosive 50-meter sprints to grueling 1500-meter endurance distance races

facts_and_myths.claim: The butterfly stroke evolved directly out of a loophole in breaststroke rules.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Swimmers discovered in the 1930s that bringing arms over the water recovered faster within breaststroke regulations before becoming its own stroke.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Butterfly was officially recognized as an independent Olympic stroke in 1956.

facts_and_myths.claim: Human hair has zero measurable impact on professional swimming speed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Swimmers shave all exposed body hair and wear hydrodynamic silicone caps because water surface friction creates measurable hydrodynamic drag.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Shaving hair also removes microscopic dead skin cells, increasing sensory feel for water flow.

name: Volleyball
visual_anchor: Mid-air vertical action shot of an athlete elevated high above the white boundary net preparing an explosive downward spike against two outstretched blockers.
core_traits: Played by two squads of six players separated by a high overhead net
Each side is allowed a maximum of three consecutive contacts before grounding or returning the ball
Common three-touch tactical sequence consists of a bump pass, a high set, and a downward spike
A designated defensive specialist called the libero wears a contrasting jersey

facts_and_myths.claim: Volleyball was originally named Mintonette when it was created in 1895.
facts_and_myths.explanation: William G. Morgan invented the game as a gentle indoor pastime for older YMCA members and called it Mintonette before a spectator noticed the volleying nature.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Morgan designed it just four years after basketball was created in the same state.

facts_and_myths.claim: The libero player is allowed to serve and spike from anywhere behind the attack line.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Under standard international FIVB rules, the libero is strictly restricted to back-row defensive play and cannot serve, block, or attack above net height.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The libero can substitute freely without counting toward team substitution limits.

name: Badminton
visual_anchor: Ultra-fast vertical shutter capture of an aerodynamic feathered shuttlecock freezing in time inches before striking an ultra-tensioned lightweight racket face.
core_traits: Racket sport where competitors strike a lightweight feathered projectile across a high net
Projectile consists of sixteen goose or duck feathers embedded into a rounded cork base
Points are scored when the projectile touches the opponent's court floor or is faulted
Known for generating the fastest projectile speeds of any racket sport in the world

facts_and_myths.claim: Smash shots in professional badminton can exceed 400 kilometers per hour.
facts_and_myths.explanation: High-speed laboratory and match tests have clocked top smashes at over 490 km/h, surpassing top Formula 1 racing speeds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The feathers on a tournament-grade shuttlecock are traditionally plucked exclusively from the left wing of a goose for aerodynamic symmetry.

facts_and_myths.claim: Badminton originated in Victorian England without any Asian ancestral roots.
facts_and_myths.explanation: British military officers in Pune, India modernized the ancient game of 'Poona' and brought it back to the Duke of Beaufort's Badminton House.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The game officially debuted as an Olympic medal sport at the 1992 Barcelona Games.

name: Table Tennis
visual_anchor: Dramatic table-level vertical shot of a lightweight hollow celluloid ball bouncing off a dark green matte surface, framed by a red rubber paddle.
core_traits: High-speed game contested on a hard tabletop divided centrally by a six-inch net
Players wield small laminated wooden paddles covered with textured rubber sheets
Games are won by the first player reaching eleven points with at least a two-point cushion
Serves must bounce once on the server's side before clearing the net to the receiver's court

facts_and_myths.claim: The phrase 'Ping Pong Diplomacy' refers to real diplomatic exchanges between the US and China in 1971.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Exhibition matches between American and Chinese players paved the way for Richard Nixon's historic visit to Beijing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The sound of the celluloid ball striking paddles and tables inspired the onomatopoeic trade name Ping Pong.

facts_and_myths.claim: Table tennis balls are filled with flammable pressurized helium.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Standard table tennis balls are filled with ordinary trapped air at normal pressure, though older celluloid models were highly combustible.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern competition balls are made of non-celluloid poly-plastic for safety.

name: Baseball
visual_anchor: Sun-drenched vertical perspective behind home plate as a wooden ash bat connects with a stitched red-seam leather ball kicking up chalk dust.
core_traits: Bat-and-ball contest played between two teams of nine taking turns batting and fielding
Batters attempt to circle four diamond-configured bases to score runs
A standard professional contest lasts nine innings without an overarching game clock
Pitchers deliver the ball from a raised central dirt mound toward the catcher's mitt

facts_and_myths.claim: Every major league baseball contains exactly 108 double hand-stitched seams.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Each regulation Major League Baseball is stitched by hand with waxed red cotton thread through 108 pierced holes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Baseballs are rubbed with a specific muddy silt harvested from a secret spot in the Delaware River before every game.

facts_and_myths.claim: Civil War hero Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown, New York in 1839.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Historical evidence demonstrates the Doubleday origin was an invented patriotic legend; baseball evolved from English folk games like rounders.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Alexander Cartwright codified the basic modern diamond rules in 1845.

name: Golf
visual_anchor: Panoramic vertical framing of an undulating manicured emerald green at dawn, a dimpled white ball tracking toward a yellow flagstick pin.
core_traits: Individual precision discipline where players strike balls into holes across natural terrain
Goal is to complete a round of eighteen holes with the lowest cumulative number of strokes
Players choose from an arsenal of specialized clubs including woods, irons, wedges, and putters
Each hole possesses a rated standard stroke expectation termed 'par'

facts_and_myths.claim: Golf is one of only two sports ever played on the surface of the Moon.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Astronaut Alan Shepard hit two golf balls using a makeshift six-iron on the lunar surface during the Apollo 14 mission in 1971.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because of lunar gravity and no air resistance, Shepard reported the second ball went 'miles and miles'.

facts_and_myths.claim: The word golf is an acronym standing for 'Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: This is a popular backronym; the name derives from medieval Dutch 'kolf' and Scots 'gouf', meaning club or bat.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mary, Queen of Scots was an avid golfer and is credited with creating the term 'caddie'.

name: Boxing
visual_anchor: Moody vertical shot of two fighters under a single hanging ring spotlight, sweat flying off leather gloves as an uppercut lands against canvas ropes.
core_traits: Combat sport where two competitors wearing padded gloves throw punches inside a square canvas ring
Regulated by the Marquess of Queensberry rules prohibiting hitting below the belt
Bouts consist of timed three-minute rounds separated by one-minute corner breaks
Can be won through knockout, technical knockout, or judges' scorecards

facts_and_myths.claim: Ancient Greek boxers wrapped their hands in leather strips called himantes rather than padded gloves.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Ancient pugilists used rawhide thongs to protect their knuckles, which later evolved into studded Roman caestus weapons.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bare-knuckle champion James Figg popularized modern prize fighting in London in 1719.

facts_and_myths.claim: Padded boxing gloves were invented primarily to prevent knockouts and brain trauma.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gloves were introduced primarily to protect fighters' delicate hand bones from fractures, allowing them to punch harder without breaking fingers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Bare-knuckle bouts actually saw fewer concussions because fighters avoided striking hard skull bones.

name: Bowling
visual_anchor: Polished hardwood lane reflection with neon alley lights framing a heavy bowling ball crashing through ten triangular white pins with red collars.
core_traits: Target sport where participants roll a weighted ball down a long oiled lane
Objective is to knock down ten pins positioned in an equilateral triangle at the lane's far end
A complete match consists of ten frames with opportunities for strikes and spares
Maximum possible score in a standard ten-pin game is 300 points for twelve consecutive strikes

facts_and_myths.claim: Archaeologists discovered ancient bowling pins and balls inside an Egyptian child's tomb dating back 5,000 years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: British archaeologist Sir Flinders Petrie unearthed primitive bowling equipment in a pre-dynastic grave at Naqada.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: King Edward III banned bowling in fourteenth-century England because soldiers were neglecting archery practice.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bowling lanes are completely dry and smooth to maximize ball glide.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Lanes are coated with intricate mineral oil patterns that dictate how and where the ball hooks toward the pocket.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Professional bowlers study oil breakdown patterns as games progress.

name: Ice Hockey
visual_anchor: Chilled ice-level vertical perspective of a vulcanized black rubber puck gliding across shaved frost, framed by steel skate blades and composite sticks.
core_traits: High-speed contact game played by two teams of six skaters on a freezing ice rink
Competitors use curved wooden or composite sticks to maneuver a vulcanized black rubber puck
Game consists of three twenty-minute periods enclosed by wooden boards and protective glass
Goaltenders wear extensive leg pads and a blocker glove to guard a small four-by-six foot goal

facts_and_myths.claim: Before vulcanized rubber was standard, early Canadian hockey matches used frozen cow dung as pucks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In nineteenth-century rural outdoor games, improvised discs like carved wood or frozen cow manure were frequently used.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern pucks are kept frozen before NHL games to prevent them from bouncing on the ice.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Stanley Cup trophy is melted down and recast with a new bowl every championship year.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The original bowl donated by Lord Stanley in 1892 sits atop rings engraved with winning players' names, with older rings retired to the Hall of Fame.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Stanley Cup has accidentally been left in a snowbank and dropped in swimming pools by celebrating players.

name: Archery
visual_anchor: Extreme vertical close-up looking down the carbon shaft of an arrow drawn back against a taut bowstring, focused on a distant circular yellow bullseye.
core_traits: Precision sport involving shooting feathered arrows from an elastic bow at a distant stationary target
Olympic target features concentric colored scoring rings with gold yellow at the center
Bullseye center yields maximum ten points at standard distances of seventy meters
Athletes wear finger tabs, arm guards, and use stabilizing counterweight rods

facts_and_myths.claim: Archery was the first sport to allow women to compete at the Olympic Games in 1904.
facts_and_myths.explanation: At the St. Louis 1904 Games, archery was the only event open to female athletes, with Lida Howell winning three gold medals.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Medieval English longbowmen could release twelve aimed arrows a minute with bows requiring over 100 pounds of draw weight.

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern Olympic arrows are solid wooden dowels fletched with eagle feathers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Competition arrows are crafted from micro-diameter carbon fiber and aluminum alloys paired with precision polymer vanes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern tournament arrows travel at speeds surpassing 200 kilometers per hour.

name: Billiards
visual_anchor: Dramatic overhead vertical shot of a chalk-tipped wooden cue stick lining up the white cue ball across baize green cloth toward a triangular cluster of numbered balls.
core_traits: Cue sport contested on a cloth-covered rectangular slate table bordered by rubber cushions
Players strike a white cue ball using a tapered wooden cue stick with a leather tip
Disciplines include eight-ball, nine-ball, carom, and twenty-two ball snooker
Pocket variants require players to sink balls into six perimeter holes

facts_and_myths.claim: Early billiard balls in the nineteenth century were manufactured from elephant ivory.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Thousands of elephants were hunted for tusks to produce ivory spheres until synthetic celluloid and phenolic resin replaced them.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A $10,000 prize offered in 1868 for an ivory substitute helped launch the commercial plastics industry.

facts_and_myths.claim: The green cloth covering billiard tables is chosen solely for decorative interior design.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Billiards evolved as an indoor adaptation of outdoor lawn games like croquet, so green baize was used to imitate natural lawn grass.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The cloth is made of a dense worsted wool blend to minimize friction.

name: Rugby
visual_anchor: Mud-splattered vertical action shot of a physical scrum collapsing forward as fifteen players push against each other under pouring rain on grass.
core_traits: High-impact contact team sport played with an oval ball across an expansive rectangular pitch
Players carry, kick, and pass backwards, with forward throwing strictly outlawed
Points are scored by grounding the ball in the opponent's in-goal area to score a try
Contested in two primary codes: Rugby Union (15-a-side) and Rugby League (13-a-side)

facts_and_myths.claim: Legend holds that schoolboy William Webb Ellis created rugby by picking up the ball during a soccer match in 1823.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The famous school legend at Rugby School in England is commemorated by the Rugby World Cup trophy bearing Webb Ellis's name.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The original rugby balls were made from inflated pigs' bladders encased in stitched leather.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rugby players wear hard composite plastic helmets identical to American football gear.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rugby rules forbid hard protective shells; players may only wear soft padded headgear called scrum caps to guard against cauliflower ear and cuts.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tackling techniques in rugby mandate wrapping arms rather than launching with shoulders.

name: Cricket
visual_anchor: Atmospheric vertical frame of a wooden three-stump wicket with flying bails backlit by golden afternoon sunlight as a hard leather red ball strikes.
core_traits: Bat-and-ball team game contested between two sides of eleven on a large oval grass ground
Action centers on a central twenty-two yard rectangular strip called the pitch
Bowlers deliver the ball with a straight arm attempting to dislodge bails atop three wooden stumps
Formats range from multi-day Test cricket to explosive three-hour Twenty20 matches

facts_and_myths.claim: Cricket is the second most popular spectator sport in the world by estimated global fanbase.
facts_and_myths.explanation: With colossal followings across India, Pakistan, the United Kingdom, and Australia, cricket claims over 2.5 billion fans globally.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The longest cricket match in history was the 1939 'Timeless Test' between England and South Africa, which lasted nine days before being abandoned so England could catch their boat home.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cricket was never included in the Olympic Games.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cricket was played at the 1900 Paris Olympics, where Great Britain won gold against France, and is scheduled to return at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The 1900 match featured players who were largely British embassy staff in Paris.

name: Surfing
visual_anchor: Breathtaking vertical shot looking out from deep inside the translucent turquoise barrel of an ocean wave as a surfer carves along the water wall.
core_traits: Surface water sport where an athlete rides on the forward face of a moving ocean wave
Riders stand upright upon lightweight composite or fiberglass surfboards
Surfers paddle into swell velocity before executing a rapid pop-up transition
Judged on speed, power, flow, and the execution of radical maneuvers like cutbacks and airs

facts_and_myths.claim: Ancient Polynesian royalty practiced surfing centuries before Europeans documented it in Hawaii.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Surfing was deeply embedded in spiritual Hawaiian culture, known as 'hee nalu' (wave sliding), where chiefs used special koa wood boards.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Olympic swimming legend Duke Kahanamoku helped popularize surfing across California and Australia in the 1910s.

facts_and_myths.claim: All surfboards are made with identical length and fin arrangements.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Boards vary dramatically, from nine-foot longboards designed for cruising to six-foot shortboards featuring thruster tri-fin setups for radical aerials.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tow-in surfers riding 70-foot monster waves use tiny, heavy boards with foot straps.

name: Skateboarding
visual_anchor: Gritty urban concrete vertical shot capturing a concave wooden deck rotating 360 degrees mid-kickflip against a sunny city skatepark ledge.
core_traits: Action sport involving riding and performing tricks on a seven-ply maple deck with polyurethane wheels
Propelled by pushing with one foot while balancing on the grip tape-covered board
Foundation of modern street tricks is the ollie, an aerial leap where board and rider rise together
Contested in street courses with stairs and rails or transition bowls with vertical curved coping

facts_and_myths.claim: Skateboarding was originally called 'sidewalk surfing' by California surfers waiting for flat ocean waves.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the 1950s, surfers nailed roller skate wheels to wooden 2x4 planks so they could practice wave-riding movements on land.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The invention of urethane wheels in 1972 revolutionized grip and shock absorption, birthing modern skate culture.

facts_and_myths.claim: An ollie requires magnets or foot straps connecting the skater's shoes to the skateboard.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The ollie is pure physics: popping the wooden tail against concrete creates upward rebound while sliding the front shoe levels the deck mid-air.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Alan 'Ollie' Gelfand invented the no-hands aerial on vert ramps in 1977.

name: Skiing
visual_anchor: Crisp alpine vertical view of a skier carving high-speed parallel turns through fresh powdery snow, leaving plumes against snow-capped peaks.
core_traits: Winter sport utilizing long narrow runners attached to boots to glide across snow
Skiers hold two pointed poles for rhythm, propulsion, and balance control
Disciplines split into Alpine downhill slalom and Nordic cross-country endurance
Athletes navigate steep mountain courses weaving through red and blue directional gates

facts_and_myths.claim: Rock art discovered in northern Scandinavia suggests humans used skis over 5,000 years ago.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Petroglyphs and preserved wooden ski fragments found in Norway and Russia date back to prehistoric hunters tracking reindeer.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The English word 'ski' comes from the Old Norse word 'skid', meaning split piece of firewood.

facts_and_myths.claim: Downhill ski wax is applied purely to protect ski bases from freezing to ice.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Wax is engineered to repel water and regulate the microscopic friction layer that melts under ski pressure, optimizing glide speed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Olympic wax technicians test dozens of specialized fluorocarbon and hydrocarbon formulas before each race.

name: Snowboarding
visual_anchor: Vertiginous vertical perspective of a snowboarder soaring upside down in a massive halfpipe invert, goggles reflecting frozen white snowbanks.
core_traits: Winter sport descending a snow-covered slope while standing sideways on a single fiberglass board
Both feet are secured inside non-releasable bindings angled across the deck
Riders carve using toe-edge and heel-edge pressure along metal steel edges
Events include halfpipe, slopestyle terrain parks, big air jumps, and boardercross

facts_and_myths.claim: The modern snowboard originated as a toy called the 'Snurfer' bound with a nose rope.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Sherman Poppen tied two skis together with a rope in 1965 so his daughters could slide down backyard hills in Michigan.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over one million Snurfers were sold as toys before Jake Burton Carpenter added bindings to create competitive snowboards.

facts_and_myths.claim: Snowboarding was instantly welcomed at all major ski resorts from the moment it was invented.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the 1970s and 1980s, the vast majority of ski resorts banned snowboarders, viewing them as rebellious and destructive to ski tracks.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Snowboarding made its official Olympic debut at the 1998 Nagano Winter Games.

name: Cycling
visual_anchor: Dynamic vertical low-angle tracking shot of a tightly packed peloton of aerodynamic carbon road bikes leaning sharply through an alpine mountain hairpin.
core_traits: Competitive locomotion using human-powered two-wheeled bicycles
Disciplines include road stage racing, track velodrome, mountain biking, and BMX
Riders utilize aerodynamic tuck positions and draft in packs to minimize wind resistance
The premier world event is the grueling three-week Tour de France covering thousands of kilometers

facts_and_myths.claim: A cyclist riding in the middle of a dense peloton expends up to forty percent less energy than a solo rider.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Aerodynamic wind tunnel tests demonstrate that drafting inside a pack drastically slashes air resistance drag.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The yellow jersey ('maillot jaune') in the Tour de France was chosen because the sponsoring newspaper was printed on yellow paper.

facts_and_myths.claim: The bicycle chain and pedal drive was part of the original 1817 German 'dandy horse' design.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Baron Karl von Drais invented the Laufmaschine (running machine) with no pedals; riders pushed their feet along the ground.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Rotary pedals connected to the front wheel weren't added until the 1860s in France.

name: Marathon Running
visual_anchor: Inspiring vertical frame looking down a wide city avenue packed with thousands of endurance runners, shoes pounding asphalt under morning mist.
core_traits: Long-distance foot race contested over an exact standard distance of 42.195 kilometers (26.2 miles)
Tests aerobic cardiovascular endurance, muscular stamina, and metabolic pacing
Elite competitors complete the distance in just over two hours at near-sprint speeds
Part of the Olympic athletics program since the inception of the modern Games in 1896

facts_and_myths.claim: The standard marathon distance of 26.2 miles was set to accommodate the British Royal Family in 1908.
facts_and_myths.explanation: At the 1908 London Olympics, the route was extended from Windsor Castle to finish directly beneath the Royal Box at White City Stadium.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Before 1908, marathon distances varied between approximately 40 and 42 kilometers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Legendary messenger Pheidippides only ran 26 miles during the Persian invasion of Greece.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Historians note Pheidippides actually ran 150 miles from Athens to Sparta to request military aid before running from Marathon to Athens.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Greek Spartathlon race retraces his original epic 153-mile route each year.

name: Gymnastics
visual_anchor: Breathtaking vertical capture of an elite gymnast frozen mid-flight performing a layout twist high above a four-inch wide wooden balance beam.
core_traits: Discipline demanding intense physical strength, flexibility, coordination, and acrobatic balance
Women compete on vault, uneven bars, balance beam, and floor exercise
Men compete on floor, pommel horse, still rings, vault, parallel bars, and horizontal bar
Routines are judged by difficulty scores combined with execution deductions

facts_and_myths.claim: Nadia Comaneci scored the first 'Perfect 10' in Olympic gymnastics history at Montreal 1976.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The electronic scoreboard displayed '1.00' because it was only built with three digits, never expecting a flawless 10.00 score.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Comaneci earned seven perfect scores during the 1976 Montreal Games at age fourteen.

facts_and_myths.claim: Gymnasts coat their hands with chalk to dry sweat and maximize slippery skin slide.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gymnastics chalk is magnesium carbonate, used to eliminate moisture while dramatically increasing surface friction and grip on apparatus bars.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Gymnasts on high bar also wear leather hand grips with wooden dowels to hook securely onto steel rails.

name: Fencing
visual_anchor: High-contrast vertical shot inside a darkened hall as two white-clad fencers lunge across a conductive metallic piste, steel blades flashing under spotlights.
core_traits: Combat sport based on traditional swordsmanship fought on a narrow fourteen-meter piste
Competitors fence using three distinct blunted weapons: foil, epee, and sabre
Athletes wear protective mesh masks, puncture-resistant jackets, and electronic scoring vests
Touches are registered instantly via electric sensors connected to scoring box lights

facts_and_myths.claim: Electronic scoring was introduced in fencing long before video replay existed in most other sports.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The epee weapon adopted electrical buzzer scoring in 1936 to eliminate judging controversies over microsecond touches.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Foil hits are registered only when pressed with a tip force exceeding 500 grams.

facts_and_myths.claim: Fencing jackets were traditionally white purely because the sport was associated with royalty.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Before electronic cords, blades were tipped with ink or soot, and white cotton uniforms allowed judges to verify touch marks clearly.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern competition uniforms are made of bulletproof Kevlar or Dyneema ballistic fabrics.

name: Judo
visual_anchor: Dynamic vertical impact frame on tatami mats as a judoka in a white heavy cotton gi executes an explosive shoulder throw, slamming the opponent down.
core_traits: Japanese martial art and Olympic combat sport founded by Jigoro Kano in 1882
Focuses on unbalancing opponents to throw them flat on their backs with speed and force
Ground grappling techniques include pins, joint locks on the elbow, and chokeholds
An immediate victory is awarded for executing a flawless throw, called an 'ippon'

facts_and_myths.claim: The word judo translates into English as 'the gentle way'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The philosophy emphasizes yielding to an opponent's force and redirecting their kinetic energy rather than resisting with brute force.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Judo was the very first Asian martial art to become an official Olympic event at Tokyo 1964.

facts_and_myths.claim: A judo black belt was originally awarded to signify that the cloth had turned dirty from years of blood and sweat.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Jigoro Kano created the belt ranking system using swimmer ranks, selecting black simply as a clean visual contrast against white cotton gis.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: High-ranking judo grandmasters wear red-and-white paneled belts or pure solid red belts.

name: Wrestling
visual_anchor: Intense vertical mat-level shot of two singlet-clad grapplers locked in a collar tie, muscles strained and sweat dripping onto the circular competition ring.
core_traits: Ancient combat sport focused on grappling, takedowns, throws, and pins without striking
Two Olympic styles: Freestyle allows attacking the legs, while Greco-Roman forbids holds below the waist
Matches consist of two three-minute periods on a padded circular foam mat
A bout concludes immediately if one wrestler pins both of the opponent's shoulders flat to the mat

facts_and_myths.claim: Wrestling has been part of every single ancient and modern Olympic Games except 1900.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It was contested at the ancient Olympic Games in 708 BC and featured at Athens 1896, missing only the 1900 Paris edition.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ancient Greek wrestlers competed completely naked and coated their skin with olive oil.

facts_and_myths.claim: Greco-Roman wrestling was the exact style practiced by ancient Roman gladiators.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The style was developed by French Napoleonic soldiers in the nineteenth century, who named it 'Greco-Roman' to add classical historical prestige.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Ancient wrestling rules permitted leg trips, unlike modern Greco-Roman rules.

name: Weightlifting
visual_anchor: Dramatic low-angle vertical shot of a lifter in a lifting suit locked beneath a bending steel barbell loaded with heavy multicolored bumper plates.
core_traits: Strength sport where athletes attempt maximum single-lift attempts with a loaded barbell
Composed of two competition lifts: the snatch and the clean and jerk
Lifters get three attempts at each movement, with the combined highest weights determining the total
Barbells are loaded with standardized color-coded rubber bumper plates dropped onto a wooden platform

facts_and_myths.claim: Olympic barbells are precision-engineered to flex and whip dynamically during heavy lifts.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Special spring steel shafts flex under explosive loads, allowing lifters to time the upward rebound when catching weights overhead.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The bearings inside Olympic barbell sleeves allow the heavy plates to spin freely so rotational inertia does not wrench lifters' wrists.

facts_and_myths.claim: Olympic weightlifting includes the bench press and deadlift as scored events.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The bench press, squat, and deadlift belong to the sport of powerlifting; Olympic weightlifting consists exclusively of the snatch and clean and jerk.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A third Olympic lift, the clean and press, was eliminated in 1972 due to judging difficulties.

name: Rowing
visual_anchor: Symmetrical vertical aerial view of an eight-person sleek carbon rowing shell slicing straight through glass-still water, eight oars pulling in flawless unison.
core_traits: Watercraft racing sport where crews propel boats through water using long wooden or composite oars
Athletes sit facing backwards toward the stern on sliding seats inside narrow shells
Disciplines split into sculling (two oars per rower) and sweep rowing (one oar per rower)
Standard Olympic regattas are sprinted over a straight 2,000-meter buoyed course

facts_and_myths.claim: The steersperson in a rowing shell, called the coxswain, does not pull an oar.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The coxswain sits in the stern facing forward, steering the rudder, coordinating race cadence, and motivating the crew through a microphone system.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Oxford-Cambridge Boat Race on the River Thames is one of the oldest sporting events in the world, dating back to 1829.

facts_and_myths.claim: Rowing relies almost exclusively on upper body and arm strength.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Over seventy percent of rowing power is generated by the legs pushing against the foot stretcher as the sliding seat rolls backwards.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Elite rowers possess some of the highest lung capacities and aerobic VO2 max values ever recorded.

name: Water Polo
visual_anchor: Intense vertical water-level frame of a player treading high above churning pool water, cocking an arm back with a textured yellow ball to fire at the cage.
core_traits: Water team sport where seven players per side swim and pass a ball to score into floating goal nets
Competitors are strictly forbidden from touching the bottom or sides of the deep pool
Players sustain position using the energy-intensive eggbeater kick technique
Field players may only catch, hold, and shoot the ball using a single hand at a time

facts_and_myths.claim: The 1956 Olympic water polo semifinal between Hungary and the USSR is known as the 'Blood in the Water' match.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Tensions from the Hungarian Revolution boiled over into physical underwater brawling, leaving Hungarian star Ervin Zador with blood streaming down his face.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hungary won the brutal 1956 match 4-0 and took home the Olympic gold medal.

facts_and_myths.claim: Water polo players wear ear guards on their caps primarily to listen to underwater coach instructions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The plastic cupped ear guards protect eardrums from rupturing if struck point-blank by high-speed balls or flailing hands.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: White caps are worn by home teams while dark caps are worn by visitors for easy referee identification.

name: High Jump
visual_anchor: Spectacular vertical slow-motion capture of an athlete arching head-first backwards over a horizontal crossbar high in the air, framed against open blue sky.
core_traits: Track and field field event where competitors jump unaided over a horizontal crossbar
Athletes launch off a single foot from a curved J-shaped synthetic runway
Competitors are eliminated after recording three consecutive failures at a given height
Standard technique is the Fosbury Flop, arching the back over the bar facing upward

facts_and_myths.claim: Dick Fosbury revolutionized the high jump at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics by leaping backwards.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While competitors used the forward straddle technique, Fosbury arched his back over the bar, winning Olympic gold and transforming the sport forever.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Fosbury Flop allows the jumper's center of mass to travel beneath the bar while their body passes over it.

facts_and_myths.claim: High jumpers are legally allowed to take off using a two-footed springboard leap.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Under World Athletics rules, jumpers must take off from exactly one single foot; launching off both feet results in an immediate red flag foul.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The men's world record stands at 2.45 meters (8 feet 0.5 inches), set by Javier Sotomayor in 1993.

name: Figure Skating
visual_anchor: Elegantly lit vertical shot of a skater spinning in a blur at center ice under a bright arena spotlight, ice shavings sparkling in a halo around their skates.
core_traits: Ice sport combining athletic jumping, rapid spinning, footwork, and musical choreography
Skated on specialized steel blades with prominent front serrated toe picks
Events include Men's singles, Women's singles, Pairs skating, and Ice Dance
Features complex multi-rotation jumps like the Axel, Lutz, Flip, Loop, and Salchow

facts_and_myths.claim: Figure skating was originally included as an event in the Summer Olympic Games before the Winter Olympics existed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Figure skating debuted at the London 1908 Summer Olympics and featured again at Antwerp 1920 before the inaugural 1924 Winter Games in Chamonix.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Axel jump is the only figure skating jump that takes off facing forwards.

facts_and_myths.claim: The sport is called figure skating because competitors must wear glamorous, figure-flattering costumes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The name stems from the original compulsory figures, where skaters had to carve precise geometric figure-eight patterns into the ice with blade edges.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Compulsory figures accounted for sixty percent of a skater's total score until phased out in 1990.

name: Rock Climbing
visual_anchor: Dizzying vertical top-down camera view of a climber clinging by fingertip crimps to an overhanging sheer rock face, chalk dust drifting down the abyss.
core_traits: Athletic discipline where participants ascend natural rock formations or artificial climbing walls
Disciplines include bouldering (short unroped walls with crash pads), lead climbing, and speed climbing
Climbers wear snug rubber-soled shoes and apply white magnesium carbonate chalk to hands
Athletes follow designated routes marked by colored plastic grips or natural rock features

facts_and_myths.claim: Sport climbing made its official Olympic debut at the Tokyo 2020 Games.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Athletes competed in a combined format spanning speed, bouldering, and lead climbing disciplines before split medals were introduced for Paris 2024.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Olympic speed climbing, competitors scale a standard 15-meter vertical wall in under five seconds.

facts_and_myths.claim: Free solo climbing means using safety ropes and bolts to pull yourself up the rock wall.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Free soloing means climbing completely alone without ropes, harnesses, or safety protection; a single slip results in a lethal fall.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Alex Honnold completed the first free solo ascent of El Capitan's 3,000-foot wall in 2017.

name: Karate
visual_anchor: Striking vertical composition of a martial artist executing a sharp snapping reverse punch inside a traditional wooden dojo, white gi snapping with kinetic power.
core_traits: Striking martial art developed on the Ryukyu Islands of Okinawa, Japan
Combines punching, kicking, knee strikes, elbow strikes, and open-hand techniques
Competition splits into kata (choreographed forms) and kumite (sparring against an opponent)
Practitioners wear a white uniform (karategi) secured with a rank-indicating colored belt

facts_and_myths.claim: The Japanese kanji characters for karate literally translate to 'empty hand'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Originally written as 'Chinese hand', master Gichin Funakoshi changed the kanji character in the 1930s to mean 'empty hand' emphasizing weaponless self-defense.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Karate made its long-awaited debut as an Olympic medal sport at Tokyo 2020.

facts_and_myths.claim: Breaking wooden boards and concrete blocks is the primary training method used in everyday dojos.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Board breaking (tameshiwari) is an occasional demonstration of focus and striking physics, while dojo practice focuses on sparring, kata, and biomechanics.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Master Funakoshi considered kata practice the ultimate soul and philosophical core of karate.

name: American Football
visual_anchor: Atmospheric vertical shot of a quarterback in full shoulder pads and a tinted helmet visor scanning the defensive line under blinding Friday night stadium lights.
core_traits: Gridiron contact sport played between two squads of eleven on a 100-yard field with end zones
Offense has four attempts (downs) to advance the pebble-grained leather ball ten yards
Points are scored via six-point touchdowns, extra points, field goals, or two-point safeties
Players wear specialized helmets, face masks, and internal shoulder pads

facts_and_myths.claim: The NFL Super Bowl is the single most watched annual television broadcast in the United States.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Annual viewership consistently exceeds 110 million viewers, commanding commercial advertising rates exceeding seven million dollars per thirty seconds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: An estimated 1.45 billion chicken wings are consumed across America on Super Bowl Sunday.

facts_and_myths.claim: American footballs have always been crafted from real pig hide.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While historical bladders came from farm pigs, regulation modern footballs are made strictly from cowhide leather with synthetic laces.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The ball's iconic pointed prolate spheroid shape was designed to facilitate aerodynamic spiral forward passes.

name: Long Jump
visual_anchor: Side-profile vertical high-speed shot of an athlete suspended horizontally over a sand pit at the peak of their hitch-kick flight, sand exploding on landing.
core_traits: Track and field event where athletes sprint down a runway and leap as far as possible into a sand pit
Jump is measured from the front edge of a twenty-centimeter wooden takeoff board to the nearest sand mark
Stepping over the foul line on the wooden board invalidates the jump with a red flag
Jumpers use in-air aerodynamic techniques like the sail, hang, or hitch-kick

facts_and_myths.claim: Ancient Greek long jumpers held heavy stone or lead weights called halteres in their hands while leaping.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Athletes swung the weights forward on takeoff and flung them backward in mid-air to increase momentum and jump distance.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mike Powell set the unbroken men's world record of 8.95 meters (29 feet 4.25 inches) at the 1991 World Championships in Tokyo.

facts_and_myths.claim: The jump distance is measured from where the athlete's toes first hit the sand.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Measurement is taken from the foul board to the closest point of contact made in the sand by any part of the body, including falling hands or hair.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If an athlete lands on their feet but falls backward onto their hands, the measurement is taken from the hand mark.

name: Taekwondo
visual_anchor: Electrifying vertical action freeze of a martial artist mid-air delivering a spinning 360-degree hook kick against electronic chest gear under tournament lights.
core_traits: Korean martial art renowned for explosive head-height kicks, jumping spinning kicks, and fast footwork
Name translates to 'the way of the foot and fist'
Competitors wear a white dobok, protective headgear, and electronic chest hogu armor
Points are awarded automatically by electronic sensors detecting contact force on head and trunk

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern Olympic taekwondo matches use wireless electronic sensors inside socks and chest protectors.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Electronic Scoring System (ESS) was adopted in 2012 to remove judging subjectivity by registering impact force automatically.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Spinning kicks to the head score the highest points in competition, earning up to five points.

facts_and_myths.claim: Taekwondo was created in ancient Korea thousands of years ago in its exact modern Olympic form.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While tracing roots to ancient martial arts like Taekkyeon and Subak, modern Taekwondo was unified by Korean martial arts masters in the 1950s.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It debuted as an official Olympic medal sport at the Sydney 2000 Olympic Games.

name: Polo
visual_anchor: Dramatic low-angle vertical shot of a galloping thoroughbred horse kicking up turf grass as a rider leans from the stirrup with a long bamboo mallet.
core_traits: Mounted equestrian team sport contested on a massive nine-acre grass field
Two teams of four mounted riders use long flexible bamboo mallets to strike a wooden or plastic ball
Matches are divided into seven-minute periods of fast play known as chukkas
Players must change horses after chukkas to protect animal stamina and health

facts_and_myths.claim: Polo originated over two thousand years ago in ancient Persia as a training exercise for cavalry troops.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Persian kings and elite royal guards played the game, known as 'chovgan', to simulate battlefield riding maneuverability.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Polo grounds are the largest field in organized sport, measuring 300 yards long by 160 yards wide.

facts_and_myths.claim: Players can hold their polo mallets with either their left or right hand.
facts_and_myths.explanation: For safety reasons to prevent catastrophic head-on horse collisions, all polo players must wield the mallet exclusively with their right hand.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Left-handed play was officially outlawed in competitive polo in 1975.

name: Speed Skating
visual_anchor: Extreme vertical angle of skaters crouched in skinsuits leaning at acute 45-degree angles around an ice oval curve, fingertips skimming the glassy ice.
core_traits: Competitive ice racing discipline on long track 400-meter ovals or tight short track 111-meter rinks
Skaters wear ultra-thin skin-tight aerodynamic suits and low-cut stiff boots
Long-track racers use clap skates where the blade detaches at the heel to prolong ice contact
Contested in pairs racing against the clock or chaotic multi-skater mass-start packs

facts_and_myths.claim: Clap skates, which allow the blade to snap open from the boot heel, shattered world records overnight.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Introduced by Dutch scientists in the mid-1990s, clap skates kept the blade on the ice longer during calf extension, lowering records instantly.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Short track skaters wear reinforced Kevlar cut-resistant gloves and place fingertips on the ice while banking around turns.

facts_and_myths.claim: Speed skaters sharpen their blades with curved hollow grooves identical to hockey skates.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Speed skating blades are ground completely flat and razor-sharp at 90-degree angles to maximize glide speed and minimize friction.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Blades are often bent slightly with a curve matching the radius of the turn.

name: Kayaking
visual_anchor: Vertical action shot of a slender fiberglass kayak cutting through roaring white foam rapids, the paddler leaning hard with a double-bladed carbon paddle.
core_traits: Paddle sport where an athlete navigates water seated inside a closed-cockpit craft
Propelled using a double-bladed paddle dipped alternately on left and right sides
Paddler wears a waterproof spray skirt stretched over the cockpit rim to seal out water
Disciplines range from flatwater sprint racing to navigating raging whitewater slalom gates

facts_and_myths.claim: The Inuit and Aleut people originally crafted kayaks from driftwood frames covered with animal seal skins.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The word 'kayak' means 'hunter's boat' or 'man's boat', designed for stealthy arctic seal and whale hunting.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The 'Eskimo roll' maneuver was developed so hunters could right themselves instantly if capsized in freezing arctic waters.

facts_and_myths.claim: A kayak and a canoe are completely identical watercraft with identical paddles.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Kayakers sit low with legs extended and use double-bladed paddles, whereas canoeists kneel or sit higher and use single-bladed paddles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Olympic whitewater slalom courses pump thousands of gallons of water per second down artificial concrete channels.

name: Handball
visual_anchor: Explosive vertical frame of a player soaring horizontally through the air above the six-meter goal crease, releasing a lightning-fast throw into the net corner.
core_traits: Fast-paced team sport where two teams of seven pass a ball using hands to throw into the opponent's goal
Contested on a forty-by-twenty meter indoor court with two thirty-minute halves
Players can take up to three steps with the ball and hold it for up to three seconds without dribbling
Only the defending goalkeeper is permitted inside the circular six-meter goal crease area

facts_and_myths.claim: Competitive handball games frequently see combined scores exceeding fifty to sixty goals per match.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Due to strict passive-play rules and quick transition counters, elite international matches are exceptionally high-scoring and relentless.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Players coat their fingers with sticky pine resin wax to improve grip and execute curve shots.

facts_and_myths.claim: Handball was originally created as an outdoor eleven-a-side game on full soccer pitches.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Field handball was played outdoors on grass pitches at the 1936 Berlin Olympics before moving permanently indoors to modern seven-a-side.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The indoor transition protected games from bad winter European weather.

name: Chess
visual_anchor: Moody vertical cinematic closeup of a polished wooden King piece standing upon an ebony square, surrounded by defeated pawns under soft directional rim lighting.
core_traits: Two-player abstract strategy game played on an eight-by-eight checkered board of 64 alternating squares
Each player commands sixteen pieces: one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns
Ultimate objective is to trap the opposing king into an inescapable attack called checkmate
Knights possess a unique L-shaped movement pattern and are the only pieces capable of jumping over others

facts_and_myths.claim: Chess evolved from an ancient Indian strategy game called Chaturanga created in the sixth century.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Chaturanga represented the four divisions of the Indian military: infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariotry, spreading to Persia as Shatranj.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The phrase 'Checkmate' comes from the Persian 'Shah mat', meaning 'the King is helpless' or 'the King is dead'.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Queen piece was always the most powerful piece on the board since the game's earliest origins.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In ancestral Persian chess, the piece was the vizier (counselor), moving only one single square diagonally; the modern omnidirectional Queen emerged in fifteenth-century Europe.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Queen's empowerment in Spain coincided with the reign of Queen Isabella I.

name: Checkers
visual_anchor: Vertical macro perspective of stacked ridged wooden discs on dark board squares, with a single crowned king piece leading a multi-jump diagonal sequence.
core_traits: Two-player strategy board game played with uniform cylindrical discs on an eight-by-eight checkered grid
Pieces move strictly diagonally and capture enemy pieces by leaping over them onto adjacent vacant squares
Reaching the opposite end of the board crowns a regular piece into a king capable of backward movement
Game is won by capturing all opposing pieces or leaving the opponent with no legal moves

facts_and_myths.claim: Computer scientists have completely solved the game of checkers, proving it always ends in a draw with perfect play.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 2007, researcher Jonathan Schaeffer's program 'Chinook' computed all 500 billion billion positions over eighteen years to mathematically prove the draw outcome.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chinook is the first computer program to win a human world championship in any game.

facts_and_myths.claim: In standard English checkers, jumping an opponent's piece is an optional casual choice.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Official tournament rules strictly enforce mandatory capturing; if a jump is available, the player must take it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Older casual rules allowed 'huffing', where a player who missed a mandatory jump had their piece confiscated.

name: Rubik's Cube
visual_anchor: Glossy vertical macro shot of a partially twisted 3x3 rotational cube, vibrant primary colored stickers catching rim lighting against an out-of-focus background.
core_traits: 3D mechanical combination twisty puzzle featuring six faces covered by nine colored stickers each
Internal pivot mechanism allows each face to turn independently, scrambling colors across all sides
Solved state requires restoring each of the six faces to a uniform solid color
Possesses over 43 quintillion possible scrambling configurations but can always be solved in 20 moves or fewer

facts_and_myths.claim: Any scrambled Rubik's Cube can theoretically be solved in twenty moves or fewer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mathematically proven in 2010 using supercomputer clusters, the maximum number of moves required from any position is twenty, known as 'God's Number'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Hungarian architecture professor Erno Rubik originally built the prototype in 1974 to help students understand three-dimensional geometry.

facts_and_myths.claim: Erno Rubik solved his newly invented scrambled cube within thirty seconds on his first try.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Rubik scrambled his prototype and had no idea if it could ever be returned to order, taking an entire month of struggle to solve it for the first time.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Modern human speedcubers can solve it in under 3.2 seconds.

name: Dominoes
visual_anchor: Curved vertical line of black resin domino tiles standing upright on end on a polished table, milliseconds before a finger triggers a cascading toppling chain reaction.
core_traits: Tile-based gaming system played with rectangular pieces divided into two square ends
Each end is marked with a number of indented dots (pips) or left completely blank
A standard double-six set contains twenty-eight unique tiles ranging from 0-0 to 6-6
Players match matching pip counts end-to-end to form branching layouts on the table

facts_and_myths.claim: Domino tiles are traditionally nicknamed 'bones' because historic sets were carved from animal bone and ivory.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Eighteenth-century artisans crafted the tiles from polished animal bone backed with dark ebony wood fastened by brass pins.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The word 'domino' likely derives from a French hooded masquerade cloak that was black on the outside and white on the inside.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dominoes were invented in Europe during the Italian Renaissance.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Written historical records prove domino tiles originated in Song Dynasty China in the twelfth century before arriving in Italy centuries later.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Traditional Chinese dominoes use cards and tiles without blank faces.

name: Monopoly
visual_anchor: Vertical tabletop closeup focusing on a miniature silver metal top hat token parked on a dark blue Boardwalk tile, surrounded by miniature green houses and paper currency.
core_traits: Real-estate economics board game where players roll two dice to move around a square perimeter track
Players purchase streets, utilities, and railroads, constructing houses and hotels to bankrupt rivals
Features iconic corner spaces: GO, In Jail/Just Visiting, Free Parking, and Go to Jail
Utilizes Chance and Community Chest card decks that reward cash windfalls or impose penalty taxes

facts_and_myths.claim: Monopoly was originally invented as an anti-capitalist critique called The Landlord's Game.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Feminist Georgist Lizzie Magie patented the game in 1904 to illustrate how rent enrichment by monopolists impoverishes tenants.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During World War II, British intelligence sent special Monopoly sets to POWs containing real currency, compasses, and silk escape maps hidden inside.

facts_and_myths.claim: Official Monopoly rules state that all tax and penalty money is placed in the center for Free Parking winners.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Official rules state Free Parking is strictly a neutral resting space with zero payout; the jackpot cash pot is a widespread house rule that makes games drag on for hours.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Official rules also require unbought properties to be auctioned immediately to the highest bidder.

name: Scrabble
visual_anchor: Tactile vertical view of polished wooden alphabet letter tiles arranged on a gridded board, landing across a red Triple Word Score premium square.
core_traits: Word board game for two to four players scoring points by forming interlocking crossword-style words
Played with 100 letter tiles drawn from a fabric pouch, each tile carrying a point value based on frequency
Points multiply across premium squares such as Double Letter, Triple Letter, and Triple Word
Using all seven tiles from the player's wooden rack in a single turn scores a 50-point 'bingo' bonus

facts_and_myths.claim: Architect Alfred Mosher Butts calculated letter tile values by analyzing the front page of The New York Times.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Butts performed statistical frequency counts on newspaper copy to determine how many vowels and consonants to include and which letters (like Q and Z) should be worth 10 points.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Scrabble was originally titled 'Lexiko' and later 'Criss-Cross Words' before being trademarked in 1948.

facts_and_myths.claim: Nigel Richards, the greatest Scrabble player in history, won the French World Championship because he is fluent in French.
facts_and_myths.explanation: New Zealander Nigel Richards does not speak French at all; he memorized the entire official French Scrabble dictionary in nine weeks and won the title purely via pattern recall.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Richards has also won world titles in English and Spanish.

name: Jenga
visual_anchor: Nerve-wracking vertical perspective looking up at a towering 54-block wooden tower swaying precariously as two delicate fingers slide a middle block free.
core_traits: Physical dexterity party game played with fifty-four identical rectangular wooden hardwood blocks
Tower starts eighteen stories high with three blocks per layer oriented in alternating directions
Players take turns removing one block from any level below the top and placing it on the summit using only one hand
Game ends the exact moment any part of the structure collapses, with the loser causing the fall

facts_and_myths.claim: The name Jenga is derived from the Swahili word meaning 'to build'.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Game creator Leslie Scott grew up in East Africa playing a block-stacking family game and trademarked the Swahili verb 'kujenga' in 1983.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The record for the highest Jenga tower ever built in competition is forty-four complete levels.

facts_and_myths.claim: All fifty-four Jenga blocks are manufactured to mathematically identical microscopic dimensions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Blocks have tiny intentional micro-variations in thickness and smoothness, creating unpredictable loose and tight spots that make the puzzle challenging.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Blocks are made from genuine Alder hardwood harvested in North America.

name: Playing Cards
visual_anchor: Crisp vertical slow-motion capture of a deck of plastic-coated cards riffling together in an elegant casino bridge shuffle, revealing red hearts and black spades.
core_traits: Standard deck containing fifty-two cards divided into four distinct suits: Spades, Hearts, Diamonds, and Clubs
Each suit comprises thirteen ranks: Ace, numbers two through ten, and face cards Jack, Queen, and King
Includes two decorative Joker cards frequently used as wild cards or trump indicators
Serves as the foundation for hundreds of classic card games including Poker, Blackjack, Bridge, and Rummy

facts_and_myths.claim: The 52 cards in a standard deck correspond mathematically to the 52 weeks in a solar calendar year.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Card historians note the four suits represent the four seasons, thirteen cards per suit match lunar cycles, and summing all card values equals 365 days (366 with a Joker).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The King of Hearts is the only king depicted without a mustache and appears to push a sword into his head, earning the nickname 'the Suicide King'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Playing cards originated in medieval France alongside court nobility.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Paper playing cards originated in Tang Dynasty China during the ninth century before traveling through Mamluk Egypt into fourteenth-century Europe.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The French popularized the iconic simplified suits (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs) because they were cheaper to stencil print.

name: Six-Sided Dice
visual_anchor: Dynamic vertical macro shot of two sharp-edged casino dice tumbling across green felt, white pips glowing under low craps table illumination.
core_traits: Small throwable polyhedral cubes with six numbered faces used for generating random numbers
Faces are marked with one to six circular indented dots known as pips
Opposite faces on a standard western die always sum mathematically to seven (1+6, 2+5, 3+4)
Essential probability engine for board games, tabletop roleplaying games, and casino craps

facts_and_myths.claim: The oldest dice known to history were made from carved sheep and goat ankle bones called knucklebones.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Astragali (talus ankle bones) have four distinct naturally landing sides and were used for divination and gambling throughout Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The 5,000-year-old Royal Game of Ur excavated in Iraq included pyramidal four-sided dice.

facts_and_myths.claim: Drilling pips into a standard board game die has zero effect on its mathematical balance.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Standard cheap dice have more material scooped out of the 6-face than the 1-face, making the 6-face slightly lighter and slightly more likely to land facing down (favoring 1).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Casino dice use flush-filled pips of identical density and sharp razor edges to ensure exact 1-in-6 probability.

name: Poker
visual_anchor: Cinematic vertical closeup of a player sliding a massive tower of ceramic clay casino chips into the center pot, cards face down beside dark sunglasses.
core_traits: Family of gambling card games combining card valuation strategy, psychology, and bluffing
Players bet chips into a central pot based on the strength of their concealed five-card hands
Standard hierarchy ranks hands from high card, pair, three-of-a-kind, straight, flush, full house, up to royal flush
Texas Hold'em gives each player two hole cards and five shared community cards dealt across flop, turn, and river

facts_and_myths.claim: The dead man's hand in poker folklore consists of two black aces and two black eights.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Old West folk hero Wild Bill Hickok was holding aces and eights when he was shot in the back of the head during a poker game in Deadwood in 1876.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The fifth card Hickok held remains a subject of historical debate and mystery.

facts_and_myths.claim: A poker face requires players to remain completely motionless and never speak at the table.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Elite poker players frequently talk, joke, and display animated body language to induce behavioral tells or misdirect opponents rather than staying silent.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Table talk is considered an active psychological art in no-limit tournament play.

name: Darts
visual_anchor: Dramatic vertical closeup down the flight path of a brass dart with nylon flights embedding dead center into a red sisal bullseye ring.
core_traits: Target sport where pointed hand-thrown missiles are aimed at a circular sisal fiber board
Board is divided into twenty numbered pie-slice sections with outer double and inner triple scoring rings
Standard game is 501, where players subtract scores down to zero and must finish on a double
Competitors stand behind a designated throwing line called the oche at a distance of 7 feet 9.25 inches

facts_and_myths.claim: The highest possible score with a single turn of three darts is 180 points.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Landing all three darts in the narrow inner red band of the twenty segment yields 3 x 60 = 180 points.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A perfect leg of 501 can be achieved in a minimum of nine darts.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dartboards are constructed from compacted animal horsehair.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Quality dartboards are made from millions of compressed sisal plant fibers harvested from the agave cactus, which heal naturally after darts are pulled.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Early medieval boards were sliced cross-sections of oak tree trunks.

name: Foosball
visual_anchor: Vertical action shot looking down an illuminated green table pitch as miniature plastic figures mounted on chrome steel rods kick a white ball.
core_traits: Tabletop game modeled after association football using mounted figures on rotating steel rods
Players twist and slide rods to pass and shoot a small solid ball toward opposing goal slots
Each side controls eight rods with specific configurations of forwards, midfielders, defenders, and goalkeepers
Spinning rods a full 360 degrees without touching the ball is an illegal penalty foul in official rules

facts_and_myths.claim: Spinning the rods continuously is strictly prohibited under international tournament foosball rules.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The International Table Soccer Federation classifies spinning rods more than 360 degrees before or after striking as an illegal infraction.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tournament players wrap their handles with tennis racket grip tape for microsecond control.

facts_and_myths.claim: Foosball was invented in the United States during the 1970s disco arcade boom.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Patents for table football date back to the 1890s in Europe, with notable patents by Lucien Rosengart in France and Harold Thornton in the UK in 1921.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Thornton was inspired by a box of matches laid across his living room table.

name: Air Hockey
visual_anchor: Glowing vertical arcade shot of a neon-red polycarbonate puck floating effortlessly across a perforated white surface, defended by a plastic striker mallet.
core_traits: Fast-reaction tabletop game played across a smooth surface perforated with thousands of micro air jets
Air cushion dramatically reduces friction, allowing a circular plastic puck to glide at high velocities
Two competitors hold handheld plastic mallets (strikers/pushers) to defend their goal slit and attack
First player to score seven goals wins the regulation match

facts_and_myths.claim: Air hockey was invented by billiard table engineers working for the Brunswick corporation in 1969.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Engineers Phil Crossman, Bob Kendrick, and Brad Baldwin designed the air cushion table as an experimental frictionless game system.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The United States Air-Table-Hockey Association was founded in 1975 to standardize competitive tournament rules.

facts_and_myths.claim: Players are allowed to slam their mallet directly on top of the puck to trap it anywhere on the table.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Under USAA rules, trapping or 'topping' the puck by placing the striker over it is a foul unless the puck is airborne.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pucks can reach bank-shot speeds exceeding 80 miles per hour on tournament tables.

name: Mahjong
visual_anchor: Atmospheric vertical top-down shot of green-backed melamine tiles arranged in a fortress wall, hands revealing bamboo, character, and wind tiles.
core_traits: Tile-based game developed in nineteenth-century China played by four players around a square table
Set contains 144 tiles based on Chinese characters and symbols across suits: Bamboo, Characters, Dots, Winds, and Dragons
Players draw and discard tiles to assemble melds of three (pungs/chows) and a concluding pair (eyes)
Winning is declared by completing a fourteen-tile hand and calling out 'Mahjong'

facts_and_myths.claim: The word Mahjong originally translates to 'sparrow' in regional Chinese dialects.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The game was called 'maque' (sparrow) because the clacking sound of shuffling tiles resembles the chattering of birds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mahjong was banned during the Chinese Cultural Revolution in 1966 before being declared an official Olympic sport by China's State Sports Commission in 1998.

facts_and_myths.claim: The matching solitaire computer game with stacked tiles is the authentic ancient way Mahjong is played.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mahjong Solitaire was created as a computer puzzle by Brodie Lockard in 1981; authentic Mahjong is a four-player rummy-style strategy game.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Western Mahjong was standardized by Joseph Babcock in the 1920s with English rules.

name: Backgammon
visual_anchor: Warm vertical perspective of an inlaid wooden case displaying twenty-four alternating red and oak points, two dice rolling beside circular checkers.
core_traits: Ancient two-player board game played on a board with twenty-four narrow triangles called points
Each player moves fifteen checkers along points according to rolls of two dice
Goal is to move all fifteen checkers into the home board and then bear them off first
Features a doubling cube that allows players to raise point stakes during favorable board states

facts_and_myths.claim: Excavations in the Burnt City in southeastern Iran uncovered a 5,000-year-old board resembling backgammon.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Archaeologists unearthed an ebony board with sixty playing pieces and turquoise dice dating back to 3000 BC.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Roman emperors including Claudius and Nero were obsessive players of the precursor game Tabula.

facts_and_myths.claim: Backgammon is pure luck because dice determine every single move.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While dice introduce statistical variance, long-term mastery relies on advanced mathematical probability, pip counts, and doubling cube theory.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Top neural-net AI programs proved that expert doubling cube decisions often swing match win probabilities by double digits.

name: Connect Four
visual_anchor: Bright vertical perspective of a blue vertical plastic grid suspended in front of a window, a red checker dropping into the center column to seal a diagonal four.
core_traits: Two-player connection game played on a vertical upright plastic grid with seven columns and six rows
Players alternate dropping colored discs (traditionally yellow and red) from the top into slots
Discs fall straight down under gravity, occupying the lowest available space in the chosen column
Objective is to be the first to form a horizontal, vertical, or diagonal line of four matching discs

facts_and_myths.claim: Connect Four is mathematically solved, meaning the first player can force a guaranteed win.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mathematician James D. Allen solved the game in 1988, proving that player one can always force a win with perfect play starting in the center column.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If the first player plays anywhere other than the center column on turn one, player two can force a draw or win.

facts_and_myths.claim: Legend says British explorer Captain James Cook invented Connect Four during his naval voyages.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The tale that Captain Cook spent hours in his cabin playing 'The Captain's Mistress' is an unsubstantiated twentieth-century marketing legend.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Milton Bradley officially released the modern commercial game in 1974.

name: Twister
aliases: The Game That Ties You Up in Knots
visual_anchor: Overhead vertical angle of an expansive white vinyl floor mat covered with large red, blue, yellow, and green circles, tangled limbs stretching across colors.
core_traits: Party game played on a large plastic mat spread across the floor featuring four rows of colored circles
An analog spinner dictates limb placements, calling out combinations like 'right hand red' or 'left foot green'
Players must keep their limbs on designated colored circles without touching the floor with knees or elbows
A player who falls or lets their body touch the vinyl mat surface is eliminated

facts_and_myths.claim: Twister became an overnight sensation after Johnny Carson played it with Eva Gabor on The Tonight Show in 1966.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Before the televised broadcast, retailers refused to stock Twister calling it 'sex in a box', but Carson's playful on-air demonstration sold three million sets in a year.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Twister was the first board game where the human body acted as the playing piece.

facts_and_myths.claim: Twister was originally designed as a promotional contest for shoe polish companies.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Inventors Charles Foley and Neil Rabens created it as a body-action game originally titled 'Pretzel' before Milton Bradley acquired and renamed it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The game was inducted into the National Toy Hall of Fame in 2015.

name: Chess Clock
visual_anchor: Vertical macro focus on a modern digital chess clock sitting beside a board, large red plungers and glowing LED digits ticking down in sudden-death blitz.
core_traits: Specialized timing device consisting of two adjacent connected clocks with buttons on top
Pressing the button on one clock stops the player's countdown and immediately starts the opponent's timer
Ensures neither player consumes unfair thinking time and enforces tournament time controls
Modern digital models support incremental time delays, famously designed by Bobby Fischer

facts_and_myths.claim: World Champion Bobby Fischer patented a digital chess clock system that adds bonus seconds after each move.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fischer was granted U.S. Patent 4,884,255 in 1989 for a clock that adds incremental bonus time per turn, eliminating extreme time-scramble blunders.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Fischer Increment is now the universal standard in World Chess Championship matches.

facts_and_myths.claim: Before clocks, players were legally required to move within sixty seconds on every single turn.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In early nineteenth-century chess, games had zero time limits; players occasionally took eight to twelve hours on a single move until opponents fell asleep.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mechanical tumbling-lever clocks were first used at the London 1883 tournament.

name: Roulette Wheel
visual_anchor: Hypnotic vertical closeup looking down into a spun polished mahogany roulette bowl, an ivory ball rattling over numbered brass frets and red and black pockets.
core_traits: Casino gambling device featuring a revolving bowl with thirty-seven or thirty-eight numbered pockets
A croupier spins the wheel in one direction and sends a small white ball rolling in the opposite direction
Pockets alternate between red and black numbers from 1 to 36, with green 0 (and double 0 in American style)
Players bet on numbers, colors, odd/even, or number groupings on an adjacent green felt layout

facts_and_myths.claim: Adding all the numbers from 1 through 36 on a roulette wheel equals exactly 666.
