facts_and_myths.explanation: Summing 1 to 36 yields 666, which gave rise to the legendary casino myth that inventor Francois Blanc made a pact with the Devil for the game's secret.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Mathematician Blaise Pascal inadvertently created an early roulette mechanism while attempting to construct a perpetual motion machine in 1655.

facts_and_myths.claim: If a roulette wheel lands on black ten times in a row, the next spin is practically guaranteed to be red.
facts_and_myths.explanation: This classic error is known as the 'Gambler's Fallacy'; each spin is a completely independent random event with unchanged odds on every trial.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In Monte Carlo in 1913, black came up twenty-six times in a row, costing gamblers millions who bet against it.

name: Carrom
visual_anchor: Overhead vertical perspective of a slick wooden carrom board, a heavy acrylic striker disc flicked by a finger toward a cluster of wooden carrom men and red Queen.
core_traits: Strike-and-pocket tabletop game widely popular across South Asia played on a polished square plywood board
Players flick a heavier plastic striker disc using their fingers to knock smaller wooden discs into corner pockets
Pieces consist of nine white discs, nine black discs, and a single high-value red disc called the Queen
To claim the Queen, a player must immediately pocket another carrom man on the next shot as 'cover'

facts_and_myths.claim: Carrom players sprinkle fine boric acid or potato starch powder across the board to lubricate sliding discs.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Superfine powder eliminates wood surface friction, allowing striker discs to glide like hockey pucks on ice.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The International Carrom Federation hosts biennial world championships with players from over twenty countries.

facts_and_myths.claim: Players are allowed to reach across the board and flick the striker from any corner angle.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Official rules mandate that the striker must be placed touching both baseline guidelines and can only be flicked with a finger from behind the player's side.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Carrom is often called 'finger billiards' because of identical angle and rebound physics.

name: Go (Board Game)
visual_anchor: Serene vertical shot looking down at an untreated solid Kaya wood grid, smooth black slate and white clamshell stones intersecting lines across an expansive board.
core_traits: Ancient abstract strategy game played on a 19x19 grid of intersecting lines using black and white stones
Players take turns placing stones onto line intersections (points) rather than squares
Objective is to surround more board territory and empty intersections than the opponent
Stones with all orthogonal liberties removed are captured and permanently removed from the board

facts_and_myths.claim: The number of legal board positions in Go exceeds the total number of atoms in the observable universe.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Go has an estimated 10 to the 170th power possible positions, vastly outstripping the universe's estimated 10 to the 80th power atoms.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo became the first AI program to defeat legendary 9-dan human champion Lee Sedol in a five-game match.

facts_and_myths.claim: Go originated in medieval Japan during the Edo samurai period.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Go was invented in ancient China over 4,000 years ago as Weiqi, considered one of the four essential arts of the Chinese scholar gentleman.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chinese legend attributes its creation to Emperor Yao as a tool to teach discipline to his son.

name: Battleship
visual_anchor: Vertical split perspective of an open gray plastic battle station case, miniature red and white pegs piercing a naval target grid above molded plastic warships.
core_traits: Two-player guessing and strategy game played on two concealed ten-by-ten lettered and numbered grids
Players secretly deploy five fleet vessels: Carrier, Battleship, Cruiser, Submarine, and Destroyer
Opponents alternate calling grid coordinates to locate and sink enemy ships (e.g., 'B-4')
White pegs mark misses in ocean water, while red pegs signal direct hits on vessels

facts_and_myths.claim: Battleship originated as a pencil-and-paper pad game played by French soldiers during World War I.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Before plastic peg cases were produced in 1967, soldiers and schoolchildren played 'L'Attaque' and paper grid games during the early 1900s.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It was one of the earliest games adapted into a commercial home video game in the late 1970s.

facts_and_myths.claim: The aircraft carrier vessel occupies six grid pegs on the standard board.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The aircraft carrier occupies exactly five holes; the battleship occupies four, the cruiser and submarine three each, and the patrol destroyer two.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The phrase 'You sank my battleship!' became one of the most famous advertising slogans of the twentieth century.

name: Clue (Cluedo)
visual_anchor: Moody vertical closeup of a miniature pewter candlestick weapon lying on the wood floor of a Victorian mansion ballroom, cards of Colonel Mustard and Miss Scarlet nearby.
core_traits: Murder mystery deduction board game set inside Tudor Mansion where players solve a crime
Players deduce three mystery variables concealed in a confidential envelope: the killer, the murder weapon, and the crime room
Features six colorful suspects: Miss Scarlet, Colonel Mustard, Mrs. White, Mr. Green, Mrs. Peacock, and Professor Plum
Contains six iconic weapons: Candlestick, Dagger, Lead Pipe, Revolver, Rope, and Wrench

facts_and_myths.claim: Clue was invented by a British factory clerk sheltering in air-raid shelters during the London Blitz.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Anthony E. Pratt invented 'Murder!' in 1944 to pass time during World War II blackouts, drawing on his love of Agatha Christie murder mystery novels.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The game is titled 'Cluedo' in the UK and Australia, combining 'clue' with the Latin 'ludo' meaning 'I play'.

facts_and_myths.claim: Players can make multiple false murder accusations without penalty until they get it right.
facts_and_myths.explanation: If a player makes an official final Accusation and checks the confidential envelope but is mistaken on even one card, they are immediately eliminated from winning.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Eliminated players must still remain seated to show cards when suggested by others.

name: Risk (Board Game)
visual_anchor: High-angle vertical view of a political world map board partitioned into forty-two territories, armies of plastic colored battalions massing on borders.
core_traits: Grand strategy board game of military diplomacy and territory conquest played across six continents
Players control armies attempting to conquer forty-two territories and eliminate all competing factions
Battles are resolved by rolling attacking and defending dice, with highest rolls inflicting casualties
Reinforcements are earned each turn based on total held territories and controlling entire continent bonuses

facts_and_myths.claim: Risk was invented by Oscar-winning French film director Albert Lamorisse.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The filmmaker behind 'The Red Balloon' created the game in 1957 under the title 'La Conquete du Monde' before Parker Brothers published it in 1959.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Holding the continent of Australia is a famous beginner strategy because it has only one vulnerable entry point (Siam).

facts_and_myths.claim: In dice combat, the attacker always wins ties when rolling identical numbers against the defender.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Official rules give all ties to the defender; if both roll a six, the defending army wins and the attacker loses a unit.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: This defensive tie-breaker compensates for defenders rolling a maximum of two dice while attackers roll three.

name: Settlers of Catan
visual_anchor: Vertical tabletop macro shot of modular hexagonal resource terrain tiles showing brick, lumber, and wheat, with wooden settlement houses and a gray robber cylinder.
core_traits: Modern German-style board game where players establish settlements on an island formed of hexagonal tiles
Players collect five natural resource cards: brick, lumber, wool, grain, and ore based on two-dice production rolls
Trading resources with other players is crucial for building roads, settlements, and upgrading to cities
First player to reach ten victory points through infrastructure development and achievement cards wins

facts_and_myths.claim: Rolling a seven triggers the Robber pawn, forcing players with over seven cards to discard half their hand.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because seven is mathematically the most common roll on two six-sided dice (16.7% probability), the Robber frequently disrupts hoarding and blocks tile production.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Catan's explosive success in 1995 launched the modern 'Eurogame' revolution across North America.

facts_and_myths.claim: Inventor Klaus Teuber was a professional game design celebrity when he created Catan.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Teuber was a quiet dental technician who designed board games as an artistic escape from his dental lab in Darmstadt, Germany.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Catan was inducted into the Games Magazine Hall of Fame in 2005.

name: Boggle
visual_anchor: Vertical angle of a 4x4 plastic grid of lettered cubes under a clear dome cover, three-minute hourglass sand draining fast as someone scribbles words on a notepad.
core_traits: Timed word search game played with sixteen cubic letter dice resting in a four-by-four square tray
Shaking the domed tray scrambles letters into randomly oriented grid positions
Players race against a three-minute sand timer to record words formed by contiguous adjacent letter cubes
Any word found by more than one player is crossed out and scores zero points during round tallying

facts_and_myths.claim: The letter Q cube in English Boggle is printed with 'Qu' together on a single face.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because the letter Q in English is almost always followed by U, game designer Allan Turoff paired them on a single face so the cube wouldn't be useless.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Boggle was invented in 1972 and became one of Parker Brothers' most popular travel games.

facts_and_myths.claim: Words can use the exact same letter cube multiple times within a single word.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Official rules state that a specific letter cube can only be used once per word; letters must connect horizontally, vertically, or diagonally in an unbroken chain.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Only words with three or more letters are eligible for points.

name: Cribbage
visual_anchor: Vertical overhead shot of a wooden cribbage board with rows of drilled peg holes and brass pegs, two hands of cards laid out scoring combinations of fifteen.
core_traits: Traditional two-player card game known for its distinctive wooden track scoring board and colored pegs
Players discard two cards each into a secret spare hand called the 'crib' belonging to the dealer
Points are pegged during play and hand scoring for pairs, runs, flushes, and combinations totaling fifteen
Goal is to be the first player to peg all the way around the track to 121 points

facts_and_myths.claim: The highest possible hand in Cribbage is worth 29 points.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A perfect 29 hand requires three fives and a jack in hand, plus the fourth five cut as the starter card matching the jack's suit.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The odds of being dealt a perfect 29 hand in a two-player game are approximately 1 in 216,580.

facts_and_myths.claim: Cribbage was created by sailors during the American Civil War.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Cribbage was invented in early seventeenth-century England by poet Sir John Suckling as an evolution of the older card game Noddy.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It is the official wardroom pastime of American submarine crews.

name: Mancala
visual_anchor: Earthy vertical shot of a hinged polished wooden board carved with twelve circular pits and two oval end stores, smooth glass pebbles dropping one by one into pits.
core_traits: Ancient family of count-and-capture turn-based strategy games played with seeds, beads, or stones
Board features two rows of small hollow pits and a larger capturing basin (store or Mancala) at each end
Players scoop all counters from a pit and 'sow' them sequentially one-by-one counterclockwise
Landing the final counter in an empty pit on the player's side captures opposing stones across the board

facts_and_myths.claim: Mancala is widely considered by historians to be one of the oldest board game systems still played today.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Carved stone rows matching Mancala layouts have been uncovered in ancient Egyptian temples, Aksumite Ethiopian ruins, and Roman outposts dating back thousands of years.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Arabic word 'manqala' literally translates to 'to move' or 'to transfer'.

facts_and_myths.claim: There is only one single universal set of Mancala rules worldwide.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mancala describes an entire family of hundreds of distinct regional variants, including Kalah, Oware, Bao, Congkak, and Omweso.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In many African cultures, playing boards were carved directly into natural rock bedrock.

name: Yahtzee
visual_anchor: Dynamic vertical shot of five ivory dice rolling out of a ribbed yellow plastic cup across a paper scoresheet, all five landing with five pips up.
core_traits: Classic probability dice game played with five six-sided dice and a specialized scorecard
Players get up to three rolls per turn, holding favorable dice while rerolling unwanted ones
Categories correspond to poker hands: three-of-a-kind, full house, small straight, large straight, and chance
Scoring five-of-a-kind earns fifty points and is shouted out as 'Yahtzee!'

facts_and_myths.claim: Yahtzee was invented in 1954 by an anonymous wealthy Canadian couple who played it aboard their yacht.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The couple created 'The Yacht Game' for friends before selling the commercial rights to entrepreneur Edwin S. Lowe in exchange for 1,000 gift sets.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 50 million Yahtzee sets are sold around the world each year.

facts_and_myths.claim: The odds of rolling a natural Yahtzee on your very first roll of all five dice are about 1 in 100.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The exact probability of rolling all five dice the same on a single initial throw is 6 in 7,776, which simplifies to 1 in 1,296 (about 0.077%).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A second Yahtzee scored in the same game earns a massive 100-point bonus.

name: Uno (Card Game)
visual_anchor: Vibrant vertical shot of glossy red, yellow, green, and blue numbered cards held in hand, a legendary Wild Draw Four card dropping onto the discard pile.
core_traits: American shedding card game played with a custom deck of 108 brightly colored cards
Players match cards from hand against the top discard card by matching number, color, or symbol
Features aggressive action cards: Skip, Reverse, Draw Two, Wild, and Wild Draw Four
A player with only one card remaining in hand must immediately shout 'Uno' or face penalty draws

facts_and_myths.claim: Uno was invented in 1971 by an Ohio barbershop owner who loved playing Crazy Eights with his family.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Merle Robbins created the colorful game on his dining room table and financed the first 5,000 printed decks by mortgaging his house.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Robbins later sold the rights to International Games for $50,000 plus ongoing royalties.

facts_and_myths.claim: Official Uno rules allow players to stack a Draw Two card on top of a Draw Two card to pass the penalty.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Uno officially confirmed on social media that Draw cards cannot be stacked under standard rules; the targeted victim must draw and forfeit their turn.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Despite the official rule, stacking Draw cards remains one of the most widely played house rules on Earth.

name: Tetris
visual_anchor: Neon-soaked vertical screen shot of a glowing cyan I-tetromino sliding into a deep narrow well, clearing four horizontal rows in an explosion of 8-bit particles.
core_traits: Legendary tile-matching puzzle video game where geometric shapes composed of four squares descend a matrix
Players rotate and translate seven distinct four-block configurations known as tetrominoes (I, J, L, O, S, T, Z)
Completing a solid horizontal line across the ten-cell matrix clears the line and awards points
Clearing four lines simultaneously using the long straight four-square cyan bar scores a 'Tetris'

facts_and_myths.claim: Tetris was created in 1984 by Soviet software engineer Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pajitnov developed the game on an Electronika 60 computer at the Soviet Academy of Sciences, inspired by pentomino puzzle toys.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The famous catchy Tetris theme song 'Korobeiniki' is a nineteenth-century Russian folk song about a traveling peddler.

facts_and_myths.claim: Alexey Pajitnov became an instant multi-millionaire in 1984 when Tetris was bundled with Nintendo's Game Boy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because Pajitnov developed the software while employed by the Soviet government, all commercial royalties belonged to the state entity ELORG until 1996.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 35 million copies of Tetris were bundled with the original Nintendo Game Boy.

name: Pac-Man
visual_anchor: Nostalgic vertical arcade monitor glow framing a yellow wedge-shaped character navigating neon-blue maze corridors, chased by four colorful ghosts.
core_traits: Pioneering 1980 arcade maze chase game developed by Namco and designed by Toru Iwatani
Player guides a circular yellow character through a maze consuming 240 pellets while avoiding four roaming ghosts
Chased by four ghosts with distinct artificial intelligence behaviors: Blinky, Pinky, Inky, and Clyde
Chomping one of four flashing Power Pellets temporarily turns ghosts vulnerable and dark blue to be eaten

facts_and_myths.claim: Game designer Toru Iwatani was inspired to create Pac-Man after taking a slice out of a round pizza.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Iwatani famously conceived the iconic wedge-mouthed character in 1979 when looking at a whole pizza with a missing slice at lunch.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Billy Mitchell achieved the first documented perfect game of Pac-Man in 1999, scoring 3,333,360 points without losing a single life.

facts_and_myths.claim: The four ghosts chase the player by following identical programming scripts.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Each ghost possesses unique algorithms: Blinky gives direct chase, Pinky ambushes four tiles ahead, Inky flanks based on Blinky's vector, and Clyde wanders away when close.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: At level 256, an 8-bit integer overflow bug corrupts the right half of the screen with garbled fruit and symbols, creating the famous 'kill screen'.

name: Space Invaders
visual_anchor: Vertical CRT arcade monitor glow showing rows of pixelated green extraterrestrial invaders marching downward step-by-step above four crumbling green defensive bunkers.
core_traits: Foundational 1978 fixed shoot-'em-up arcade game developed by Tomohiro Nishikado and released by Taito
Player controls a horizontal laser cannon moving across the screen bottom to shoot down waves of descending aliens
Alien swarm consists of five rows of eleven invaders that speed up as their numbers decrease
Player shelters behind four destructible green defensive shields while shooting passing mystery flying saucers

facts_and_myths.claim: The iconic mechanic where aliens move faster as fewer remain was an accidental hardware quirk.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The processor could render fewer alien sprites much faster on screen, so Nishikado kept the accidental acceleration because it created incredible gameplay tension.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The game's pulsating four-note bass sound effect was the first video game soundtrack that accelerated dynamically with gameplay.

facts_and_myths.claim: Space Invaders caused such severe national 100-yen coin shortages in Japan that the mint had to triple production.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While the arcade boom did see millions of 100-yen coins fed into cabinets daily, macroeconomic data shows coin production was already shifting and no government mint emergency occurred.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 300,000 Space Invaders arcade machines were manufactured worldwide.

name: Pong
visual_anchor: Minimalist vertical retro black-and-white CRT vector monitor displaying two segmented vertical paddles deflecting a square blip ball across a dashed center net.
core_traits: Historic 1972 sports simulation arcade game created by Allan Alcorn and published by Nolan Bushnell's Atari
First commercially successful video game that launched the modern video gaming industry
Two-dimensional digital table tennis simulation where two players deflect a bouncing square blip
Paddles are controlled via rotary analog dial knobs (paddles) moving vertically on left and right borders

facts_and_myths.claim: The prototype Pong coin-op machine broke down on its test run because the coin bucket overflowed with quarters.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Installed at Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale, California, the machine jammed after two weeks because patrons crammed the coin mechanism full of quarters.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pong was originally assigned to engineer Al Alcorn as a throwaway training exercise by Nolan Bushnell.

facts_and_myths.claim: Pong was the very first electronic video game ever conceived in human history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Willy Higinbotham created 'Tennis for Two' on an oscilloscope in 1958, and Ralph Baer patented electronic television gaming on the Magnavox Odyssey in 1968 before Pong was created.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Magnavox successfully sued Atari for patent infringement, forcing Atari to pay licensing royalties.

name: Snake (Retro Mobile)
visual_anchor: Monochromatic vertical view of an olive-green Nokia 3310 monochrome LCD screen, a pixelated segmented serpent turning sharply to swallow a single black dot food pixel.
core_traits: Classic mobile arcade game where the player steers an elongated line across a bordered screen
Consuming stationary food pellets causes the snake's body to grow longer and increases game speed
Movement cannot be stopped or reversed directly backwards into the body
Game ends immediately if the serpent collides with screen perimeter walls or its own trailing tail

facts_and_myths.claim: Snake was embedded on over 400 million Nokia mobile phones starting in 1997.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Programmer Taneli Armanto coded Snake for the Nokia 6110 handset, turning it into the most widely played mobile game in the world at the turn of the millennium.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Armanto received a special prize from the Mobile Entertainment Forum for his contribution to mobile gaming.

facts_and_myths.claim: The game concept was originally invented by Nokia telecom engineers.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The core gameplay concept originated in the 1976 Gremlin arcade game 'Blockade' and was popularized on home computers as 'Worms' and 'Nibbler'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Snake II on the Nokia 3310 introduced mazes and bonus insect treats.

name: Minesweeper
visual_anchor: Vertical monitor closeup of a retro gray bevel-button grid, numbered colored clues 1, 2, and 3 surrounding a red flag peg, with the yellow smiley face icon wearing sunglasses.
core_traits: Single-player logic puzzle video game played on a grid of covered gray square tiles
Clicking a tile reveals either an explosive naval mine or a number indicating adjacent hidden mines
Players use logical deduction to place red warning flags on squares containing confirmed mines
Topped by a digital timer, a remaining mine counter, and a central yellow status smiley face

facts_and_myths.claim: Microsoft bundled Minesweeper with Windows 3.1 to stealthily teach users how to right-click with a computer mouse.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1992, the mouse was new to many PC users, and Minesweeper taught mouse precision and right-click flag functionality through addictive gameplay.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Microsoft founder Bill Gates became so addicted to Minesweeper that he had it uninstalled from his personal computer to stay productive.

facts_and_myths.claim: Your very first click on a fresh Minesweeper grid can accidentally hit a mine and blow up instantly.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Official Windows Minesweeper algorithms guarantee that the very first square clicked is always completely safe, generating the mine positions only after the first click.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The world record for clearing Expert mode (99 mines) is under thirty seconds.

name: Klondike Solitaire
visual_anchor: Vertical cascading visual of the iconic Windows 95 Solitaire victory animation, cards bouncing in endless looping rainbow trails across an emerald green desktop canvas.
core_traits: Single-player card puzzle game played with a standard fifty-two card deck
Cards are dealt into seven cascading tableau columns with the top card face up
Players build columns downward in alternating red and black colors
Goal is to transfer all cards to four foundation suit piles starting from Ace up through King

facts_and_myths.claim: Microsoft Solitaire was originally programmed by an unpaid college intern in 1989.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Intern Wes Cherry coded Solitaire for Windows 3.0 during his free time, while graphic artist Susan Kare designed the iconic deck artwork.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Microsoft originally bundled Solitaire to teach users how to 'drag and drop' files using a graphical user interface mouse.

facts_and_myths.claim: Every single randomly dealt game of Klondike Solitaire is mathematically winnable.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Probability mathematicians calculate that only about 80% of dealt hands are theoretically solvable, and without seeing face-down cards, humans win only about 30% of games.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The game was inducted into the World Video Game Hall of Fame in 2019.

name: Donkey Kong (Arcade)
visual_anchor: Vertical arcade cabinet CRT view of bright red slanted industrial girders, a carpenter leaping with a hammer over rolling wooden barrels toward a giant gorilla at the summit.
core_traits: Landmark 1981 platform arcade game developed by Nintendo and designed by visionary Shigeru Miyamoto
First platformer featuring jumping mechanics, introducing characters Jumpman (Mario) and Donkey Kong
Player scales slanted construction girders and climbs ladders to rescue Pauline from a giant ape
Mario leaps over rolling wooden barrels, fireballs, and wields temporary invincibility sledgehammers

facts_and_myths.claim: Donkey Kong was originally conceived as an arcade video game starring Popeye the Sailor.
facts_and_myths.explanation: When Nintendo failed to license Popeye, Bluto, and Olive Oyl from King Features, Miyamoto substituted Jumpman, the giant ape, and the damsel Pauline.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Universal Studios sued Nintendo in 1982 claiming Donkey Kong infringed King Kong, but attorney John Kirby proved King Kong was already in the public domain.

facts_and_myths.claim: The protagonist Mario was originally designed and named as an Italian plumber.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In Donkey Kong, the character was named 'Jumpman' and was depicted as a carpenter working on a construction site, only becoming a plumber in Mario Bros. in 1983.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Jumpman was renamed Mario after Nintendo of America's Seattle landlord Mario Segale.

name: Galaga
visual_anchor: Deep-space vertical arcade CRT perspective of colorful insectoid alien formations swooping in looping flight curves against a scrolling starfield, targeted by a dual white starfighter.
core_traits: Acclaimed 1981 vertical space shooter arcade game developed by Namco as the sequel to Galaxian
Player controls a starfighter moving left and right at screen bottom firing dual photon torpedoes
Enemy insectoid aliens swoop onto screen in graceful aerobatic loops before settling into formation
Iconic 'Tractor Beam' mechanic where boss aliens can capture a player's ship to form a formidable Dual Fighter

facts_and_myths.claim: Allowing an enemy boss alien to capture your fighter with a tractor beam is a deliberate high-scoring strategy.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Shooting the boss while it dives frees the captured ship to dock alongside your current ship, creating a Dual Fighter with double firepower.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Galaga introduced 'Challenging Stages' bonus rounds where players shoot 40 looping enemies without any return fire.

facts_and_myths.claim: Galaga's starry background is a pre-recorded looping video tape inside the cabinet.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The twinkling starfield is generated dynamically in real time by dedicated hardware circuitry shifting multi-colored pixel dots downward.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A famous hardware glitch in early Galaga cabinets allows players to make all enemies stop firing bullets permanently.

name: Asteroids (Arcade)
visual_anchor: Crisp vertical capture of glowing white monochrome vector wireframe lines against pitch black, a triangular spaceship blasting an enormous polygonal rock into jagged fragments.
core_traits: Seminal 1979 multidirectional space shooter arcade game designed by Lyle Rains and Ed Logg for Atari
Rendered using sharp monochrome vector graphics on a QuadraScan CRT display
Player rotates and thrusts a triangular ship with realistic zero-gravity Newtonian momentum
Shooting large floating space boulders shatters them into medium and fast tiny rocks that wrap around screen edges

facts_and_myths.claim: Asteroids became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, knocking Space Invaders off American arcade floors.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Atari manufactured over 70,000 cabinets, with arcade operators needing giant reinforced coin boxes to handle the flood of quarters.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Asteroids was the first video game to allow players to enter three initials to record their high score on a leaderboard.

facts_and_myths.claim: The screen has physical invisible borders that stop your spaceship from flying off the edge.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Asteroids utilizes toroidal space wrapping; flying or shooting off the right side of the screen immediately wraps around to the left edge.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The ship features an emergency 'Hyperspace' button that teleports the player to a random spot on screen with a risk of exploding.

name: Street Fighter II
aliases: Street Fighter II: The World Warrior
visual_anchor: Electrifying vertical arcade monitor perspective of a glowing blue Hadouken energy fireball streaking across Suzaku Castle roof tiles toward an opposing martial artist.
core_traits: Legendary 1991 fighting arcade game developed by Capcom that codified the competitive fighting game genre
Cabinet features an eight-way joystick and six buttons configured for light, medium, and heavy punches and kicks
Introduced an international roster of eight playable World Warriors including Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li, and Guile
Pioneered special combo attacks and directional joystick motions like the quarter-circle Hadouken and Dragon Punch

facts_and_myths.claim: The multi-hit combo system in Street Fighter II was an accidental programming glitch discovered during development.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Producer Yoshiki Okamoto noticed players could cancel attack recovery frames into another hit, choosing to leave it in because it required precise timing skill.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Chun-Li made history as the very first playable female character in a one-on-one fighting video game.

facts_and_myths.claim: The mysterious character 'Sheng Long' mentioned in Ryu's victory quote was an unlockable secret boss.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It was a mistranslation of the Japanese characters for 'Shoryuken' (Dragon Punch); an Electronic Gaming Monthly April Fools' joke perpetuated the myth for decades.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Capcom eventually paid homage to the rumor by creating the character Gouken in Street Fighter IV.

name: Frogger
visual_anchor: Vertical perspective looking up an illuminated arcade screen: a bright green frog hopping across a multi-lane highway packed with speeding sedans toward a river of floating logs.
core_traits: Timeless 1981 arcade action game developed by Konami and released by Sega
Player guides frogs one by one from the screen bottom to five home lily pad alcoves at the top
First half requires dodging speeding cars, trucks, and bulldozers across a busy asphalt highway
Second half requires leaping across floating logs, turtles that dive underwater, and hungry crocodiles

facts_and_myths.claim: An episode of Seinfeld famously centered around George Costanza trying to preserve his legendary Frogger high score.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In the 1998 episode 'The Frogger', George buys an arcade cabinet to save his 860,630-point score and attempts to push it across a busy New York street.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Seinfeld producers used a real Frogger cabinet modified with a battery rig for the episode.

facts_and_myths.claim: Frogger was originally titled 'Highway Frog' when designed in Japan.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Konami's original Japanese working title was 'Frog' (Kaeru no Tabi) before Sega executive Jerry Mumma suggested the punchy English title 'Frogger'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Female frogs can be picked up along the way for extra bonus points.

name: Pinball Machine
visual_anchor: Dynamic vertical wide shot down an illuminated glass-topped playfield with blinking pop bumpers, ramps, and chrome steel ball rocketing toward twin flippers.
core_traits: Electromechanical arcade game played on an inclined glass-covered wooden playfield table
Players launch a solid chrome steel ball onto the table using a spring-loaded plunger
Dual player-controlled flipper buttons manipulate mechanical bats to keep the ball from draining down the bottom drain
Ball ricochets against rubber bumpers, wire ramps, drop targets, and illuminated score multipliers

facts_and_myths.claim: Pinball was outlawed in major American cities including New York and Chicago for over thirty years.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mayor Fiorello La Guardia banned pinball in NYC in 1942, smashing tables with sledgehammers because it was deemed mafia-linked gambling without skill.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The ban was overturned in 1976 when star player Roger Sharpe testified in court and called his exact shot on a demonstration machine to prove it was a game of skill.

facts_and_myths.claim: Bumping or shoving the physical pinball machine is completely legal with zero limits.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Machines contain an internal pendulum ring tilt sensor; excessive shaking or bumping trips the sensor, triggering a 'TILT' penalty that disables flippers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The flipper mechanism was invented in 1947 by D. Gottlieb & Co. on the 'Humpty Dumpty' table.

name: Claw Machine
visual_anchor: Nerve-wracking vertical view looking up through transparent arcade glass as a three-pronged motorized chrome claw hovers above a pile of plush toys, releasing its grip.
core_traits: Mechanical arcade amusement redemption machine consisting of a glass cabinet filled with prizes
Player operates an analog joystick and drop button to position a motorized suspended mechanical claw
Claw descends, closes its prongs around a target prize, and lifts it toward an output delivery chute
Widely popular across Japanese arcades as 'UFO Catchers' and worldwide shopping mall arcades

facts_and_myths.claim: Modern claw machines are electronically programmed to deliver full gripping power only at preset payout intervals.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Machine operator manuals explicitly detail electronic voltage settings that give full claw grip strength only once every set number of paid plays (e.g., 1 in 15).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During regular non-payout plays, the claw drops the prize mid-air as voltage drops.

facts_and_myths.claim: Claw machines originated in 1990s Japanese shopping arcades.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Steam shovel mechanical cranes date back to the 1920s in the United States, originally built as miniature candy-digger carnival machines during the construction of the Panama Canal.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Early digger machines were operated with hand cranks rather than electricity.

name: Dance Dance Revolution Machine
visual_anchor: Vibrant neon-pulsing vertical view of a dancer's sneakers stomping backlit metal stage arrows (Up, Down, Left, Right) in rhythm to scrolling neon screen arrows.
core_traits: Groundbreaking 1998 rhythm music arcade game developed by Konami featuring a physical dance pad platform
Players stand on a raised metal stage equipped with four pressure-sensitive directional arrow sensors
Arrows scroll upward on a large monitor to synchronized dance tracks, prompting timed foot stomps
Performances are judged on precision timing from 'Marvelous' and 'Perfect' down to 'Miss'

facts_and_myths.claim: DDR was officially recognized by schools and health organizations as a certified aerobic exercise machine.
facts_and_myths.explanation: DDR burns hundreds of calories per hour; states like West Virginia funded DDR machines in public school physical education curriculums to combat childhood obesity.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Expert players can execute over 500 arrow steps in a single three-minute song.

facts_and_myths.claim: The stainless steel safety bar behind the dance stage is intended only as an emergency safety guard.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While installed for safety, high-level competitive tournament players lean all their body weight on the rear bar to float their feet and execute blistering step speeds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The practice is known in the competitive rhythm community as 'bar hugging'.

name: Arcade Joystick
visual_anchor: Crisp vertical macro shot of a sleek tournament fight stick, a red ball-top lever clicked diagonally alongside six responsive 30mm convex mechanical pushbuttons.
core_traits: Iconic physical arcade input controller consisting of a pivoting directional lever and mechanical microswitch buttons
Lever pivots on a base to register four-way or eight-way directional inputs using internal electrical switches
Commonly features bat-top (American style) or ball-top (Japanese Sanwa/Seimitsu style) handles
Standard input apparatus for classic arcade cabinets and modern competitive fighting game esports

facts_and_myths.claim: The joystick was originally invented in aviation to control aircraft flight surfaces.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Early twentieth-century aviation pioneers including Robert Esnault-Pelterie created the flight stick to control an airplane's elevators and ailerons.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The term 'joystick' is believed to derive from early aviator Joyce's experimental flight controls.

facts_and_myths.claim: All arcade joysticks have smooth continuous analog sensitivity like a flight simulator stick.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Classic arcade joysticks are strictly digital; moving the stick clicks discrete on/off microswitches resting behind square or octagonal restrictor gates.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Pac-Man cabinets used physical metal plates restricting the lever strictly to four cardinal directions.

name: Gamepad Controller
visual_anchor: Ergonomic vertical shot of a matte black gaming controller resting under soft ambient RGB lighting, dual analog thumbsticks and colorful face buttons in sharp relief.
core_traits: Handheld input device designed to be held with both hands to control video games on consoles and PCs
Features a directional pad (D-pad) on the left, face action buttons on the right, and top shoulder triggers
Modern iterations incorporate dual clickable analog thumbsticks, vibration haptic feedback motors, and gyroscopes
Universal standard interface for home video gaming consoles from NES through modern PlayStation and Xbox

facts_and_myths.claim: Nintendo designer Gunpei Yokoi invented the cross-shaped Directional Pad (D-pad) in 1982.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Yokoi created the flat cross-shaped thumb button for the Game & Watch Donkey Kong handheld so it could close flat in a player's pocket.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Nintendo was granted a patent for the cross D-pad that prevented competitors from copying the exact design for over twenty years.

facts_and_myths.claim: The iconic Playstation face button symbols (Triangle, Circle, X, Square) were chosen completely at random.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Designer Teiyu Goto assigned distinct meanings: Triangle represents viewpoint/direction, Square represents a menu/document, Circle means confirm/yes, and X means cancel/no.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Western games swapped Circle and X conventions compared to original Japanese releases.

name: Game Cartridge
visual_anchor: Nostalgic vertical closeup of a gray plastic cartridge with an illustrated glossy label, gold-plated circuit board edge connector pins gleaming under warm light.
core_traits: Removable solid-state storage medium housing read-only memory (ROM) chips inside a durable plastic casing
Plugs directly into the console bus via gold-plated edge connectors, offering instant boot times with zero loading lag
Dominant software format for home consoles throughout the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s (Atari 2600, NES, SNES, Genesis, N64)
Frequently incorporated battery-backed SRAM chips to save player game progress directly on the cartridge

facts_and_myths.claim: Blowing into the bottom connector pins of a malfunctioning cartridge actually causes corrosion and damages the game.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Moisture from human breath slowly oxidizes and corrodes the copper connector pins; reseating the cartridge was what actually fixed the connection.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Nintendo officially issued warnings in user manuals against blowing into Game Paks.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Fairchild Channel F in 1976 was the first system to use interchangeable ROM game cartridges.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Engineered by Jerry Lawson, the Channel F pioneered swappable cartridges, shifting video games from dedicated fixed units to an expandable software library.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Lawson was one of the few prominent African American engineers in early Silicon Valley video game history.

name: Handheld Console
visual_anchor: Iconic vertical shot of a classic gray Game Boy held in two hands, green reflective dot-matrix screen illuminated by sunlight, A and B magenta buttons at the ready.
core_traits: Self-contained portable video game console integrating display, game controls, speakers, and battery power
Allows players to enjoy video games anywhere on the move without requiring a television set
Pioneered by Nintendo's 1989 Game Boy created by Gunpei Yokoi, running swappable Game Paks on AA batteries
Evolutionary line includes Sega Game Gear, Game Boy Advance, PlayStation Portable (PSP), Nintendo DS, and Nintendo Switch

facts_and_myths.claim: A Nintendo Game Boy survived a bomb explosion during the Gulf War and still functioned perfectly.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A soldier's charred and melted Game Boy recovered from an exploded barracks was displayed at the Nintendo World Store in NYC, still running Tetris flawlessly.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The original Game Boy could run for over thirty continuous hours on just four AA batteries due to its unbacklit screen.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Game Boy was the very first handheld electronic game ever released.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mattel released handheld LED football games in 1977, Milton Bradley launched the Microvision with swappable cartridges in 1979, and Nintendo sold millions of Game & Watch units in 1980.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 118 million units of the original Game Boy and Game Boy Color were sold worldwide.

name: VR Headset
visual_anchor: Futuristic vertical shot of a sleek matte white virtual reality headset with Fresnel lenses reflecting glowing digital worlds, framed by tracked wireless hand controllers.
core_traits: Head-mounted display device providing immersive stereoscopic 3D vision and sensory spatial simulation
Tracks user head movements in real time using 6-Degrees-of-Freedom (6DoF) inertial sensors and cameras
Equipped with twin displays and precision lenses to present independent perspectives to each eye for depth perception
Paired with motion-tracked handheld controllers enabling natural grabbing and interaction in virtual space

facts_and_myths.claim: Cinematographer Morton Heilig built a functioning multisensory VR arcade booth called the 'Sensorama' in 1962.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Sensorama featured stereoscopic 3D widescreen visuals, stereo sound, vibrating seat mechanics, and chemical scent dispensers to simulate a motorcycle ride through New York.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Computer scientist Ivan Sutherland built the first computer-driven head-mounted display, nicknamed 'The Sword of Damocles', in 1968.

facts_and_myths.claim: Virtual reality sickness is caused entirely by low screen resolution.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Motion sickness primarily stems from vestibular-ocular mismatch: your eyes detect visual movement while the fluid in your inner ear senses your physical body is sitting stationary.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Reducing display latency below twenty milliseconds dramatically cuts motion sickness rates.

name: Arcade CRT Cabinet
visual_anchor: Atmospheric vertical shot of a vintage stand-up wooden arcade cabinet in a dark alley arcade, glowing marquee light illuminating side art and curved glass CRT scanlines.
core_traits: Freestanding coin-operated wooden entertainment machine housing a cathode ray tube (CRT) monitor and printed circuit board (PCB)
Equipped with an illuminated graphic marquee header, control panel with joysticks, and coin door acceptor slots
Heavy curved glass CRT display creates natural authentic scanlines and instantaneous zero-input-lag video
Available in upright stand-up cabinets, cocktail sit-down tables, and sit-in cockpit racing configurations

facts_and_myths.claim: Classic arcade games look dramatically sharper and warmer on native CRT monitors than on modern LCD flat screens.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Pixel art was designed specifically around CRT phosphor bloom and horizontal scanline blending; raw pixel displays without shaders look unnaturally harsh.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Authentic arcade CRT tubes operate at lethal voltages exceeding 25,000 volts inside the flyback transformer.

facts_and_myths.claim: The coin mechanisms in arcade cabinets simply measure the physical weight of a dropped coin.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mechanical coin comparators test diameter, thickness, metallic alloy conductivity, and drop bounce trajectory to reject slugs and washers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Cocktail table arcade cabinets were designed in Japan so businessmen could place drinks while playing in upscale coffee shops.

name: Light Gun
visual_anchor: Striking vertical closeup of a retro gray-and-blaze-orange plastic ray-gun aimed directly at a television screen, trigger held halfway back with a sharp mechanical click.
core_traits: Pointing input peripheral shaped like a handgun used for target shooting games on television screens
Contains an internal photodiode sensor inside the barrel that detects light flashing on the television screen
Pulling the trigger paints the screen completely black for one frame, then flashes white hitboxes over targets
Iconified by the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) Zapper used in Duck Hunt and Hogan's Alley

facts_and_myths.claim: The NES Zapper light gun does not shoot out light beams, but instead receives incoming light like a camera.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The gun contains a photodiode optical sensor that reads the rapid black-and-white flash sequences painted by the television screen when the trigger is pulled.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The entire optical detection process occurs in less than one-sixtieth of a second.

facts_and_myths.claim: Classic cathode ray light guns work completely fine when plugged into modern 4K OLED televisions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Light guns rely on the exact microsecond timing of a CRT's traveling electron beam; modern digital display signal processing introduces latency that breaks the optical sensor timing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The NES Zapper was redesigned in bright neon orange in 1989 to comply with US toy firearm safety laws.

name: Duck Hunt
visual_anchor: Vertical pixel art view of bright blue skies over tall marsh grass, two mallard ducks taking flight as an infamous grinning orange hound dog peeks over the grass.
core_traits: Legendary 1984 light-gun shooter video game developed by Nintendo for the Famicom and NES
Bundled with the NES Zapper light gun, challenging players to shoot ducks launched from marsh grass
Features a hunting dog companion who retrieves downed ducks or notoriously snickers if the player misses
Offers three gameplay modes: One-Duck, Two-Ducks, and Clay Shooting disc targets

facts_and_myths.claim: A second player can plug a standard controller into Port 2 to manually steer the flying ducks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Nintendo programmed Controller 2 in Mode A to let a human friend control the duck's flight direction, a secret feature missed by millions of players.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The laughing dog has become one of the most notoriously mocked and beloved characters in gaming history.

facts_and_myths.claim: In the standard home NES release, players can shoot the laughing dog to teach him a lesson.
facts_and_myths.explanation: On the home NES console, shooting the dog is impossible; only the arcade 'Vs. Duck Hunt' bonus round permitted players to shoot the dog for comical bandaged reactions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The hunting dog made his grand playable fighting debut in Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U.

name: Breakout (Arcade)
visual_anchor: Vertical minimalist view of eight rows of multicolored bricks across the ceiling, a white ball bouncing off a horizontal paddle to punch an opening through the brick wall.
core_traits: Influential 1976 arcade action game developed by Atari and conceptualized by Nolan Bushnell and Steve Bristow
Player moves a horizontal paddle along the screen bottom to bounce a ball against colored brick layers
Hitting a brick eliminates it and scores points, with higher colored layers accelerating ball speed
Punching a hole all the way to the top allows the ball to ricochet wildly behind the wall for massive auto-scoring

facts_and_myths.claim: Apple co-founders Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak designed the hardware prototype for Breakout together.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Atari offered Jobs a bonus for reducing microchips; Jobs recruited Wozniak, who worked non-stop for four days to deliver a revolutionary low-chip design.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Jobs famously received a $5,000 bonus from Atari but told Wozniak they only received $700, giving him just $350.

facts_and_myths.claim: The original Breakout arcade machine had a vibrant multi-color RGB video display screen.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The game ran on a pure black-and-white CRT monitor; colorful rows were created by sticking strips of translucent colored cellophane tape directly over the monitor glass.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Taito's Arkanoid in 1986 popularized the genre by adding power-ups and laser paddles.

name: Centipede (Arcade)
visual_anchor: Vibrant vertical arcade CRT screen showing a bright segmented neon centipede winding rapidly downward through a dense field of colorful poisonous mushrooms.
core_traits: Classic 1981 vertically oriented shoot-'em-up arcade game designed by Dona Bailey and Ed Logg for Atari
Player controls the Bug Blaster at screen bottom using a heavy high-precision rolling trackball
Centipede winds horizontally through a dense field of mushrooms, descending one row whenever striking a mushroom
Shooting a middle segment divides the centipede into two independent independently moving creatures

facts_and_myths.claim: Centipede was one of the very first arcade blockbusters co-designed by a female programmer.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dona Bailey was one of the sole female game programmers at Atari, designing Centipede's pastel color palette and addictive trackball mechanics.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Centipede was one of the first coin-op arcade games to attract an enormous dedicated female player base.

facts_and_myths.claim: Arcade cabinets used a standard joystick to steer the Bug Blaster.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Centipede relied on an analog billiard-sized trackball, giving players silky analog precision to dodge spiders, fleas, and scorpions.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Spiders move in erratic bouncing diagonal patterns that award up to 900 points at close range.

name: Dig Dug
visual_anchor: Colorful vertical arcade screen depicting cross-section soil layers, a round white-suited character pumping air through a hose to inflate a red goggle-wearing Pooka.
core_traits: Charming 1982 maze arcade video game developed by Namco and released by Atari in North America
Player digs underground tunnels through dirt layers to eliminate subterranean monsters: Pookas and Fygars
Enemies are eliminated by using an air bicycle pump to inflate them until they pop
Players can also tunnel beneath heavy suspended boulders, dropping them down shafts to crush pursuing enemies

facts_and_myths.claim: The cheerful background music in Dig Dug only plays while the character is physically walking and digging.
facts_and_myths.explanation: If Dig Dug stands completely still, the catchy music cuts off instantly; it acts as an acoustic feedback mechanism for player movement.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Fygar is a green dragon enemy capable of breathing horizontal jets of flame through dirt walls.

facts_and_myths.claim: Dig Dug uses a pickaxe weapon to strike monsters directly.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Dig Dug wields a specialized harpoon attached to an air hose pump, inflating monsters with successive button taps until they explode.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Dig Dug's real canonical name in Namco lore is Taizo Hori, an anagram of the Japanese phrase for 'I want to dig'.

name: Out Run (Arcade)
visual_anchor: Sun-drenched vertical perspective behind a red convertible sports car speeding along palm-lined coastal roads, a blond passenger leaning back as the car drifts into curves.
core_traits: Revolutionary 1986 arcade driving game designed by Yu Suzuki and developed by Sega
Player pilots a red Ferrari Testarossa convertible through five scenic European-inspired stages before time expires
Pioneered non-linear checkpoint branching: passing through stage forks lets players choose their own route to five distinct endings
Features a dashboard radio allowing players to select their background soundtrack (Magical Sound Shower, Passing Breeze, Splash Wave)

facts_and_myths.claim: Sega manufactured deluxe motion simulator hydraulic cabinets that pitched and banked with the steering wheel.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The deluxe sit-in cabinet used electric servo motors that tilted the entire molded fiberglass chassis in response to player steering and crashes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Designer Yu Suzuki drove across Europe in a BMW 520 with a video camera to scout landscapes before building the game.

facts_and_myths.claim: Out Run is a circuit racing game where you compete against seven other numbered racing cars on a track.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Out Run is a scenic checkpoint time-trial cruising experience against everyday traffic rather than an enclosed closed-circuit track race.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Out Run was the highest-grossing arcade video game of 1987 in both Japan and the United States.

name: Time Crisis
visual_anchor: Intense vertical arcade framing of a blue blowback light gun aimed past a foot pedal at cinematic split-screen action, ducks behind concrete barriers as bullets fly.
core_traits: Cinematic rail-shooter arcade franchise created by Namco in 1995 using optical light guns
Pioneered the physical foot pedal mechanic: releasing the pedal takes cover behind obstacles to reload and avoid damage
Depressing the foot pedal steps out of cover to engage enemy soldiers before the countdown clock strikes zero
Guns feature a forceful mechanical blowback slide that physically recoils with every trigger pull

facts_and_myths.claim: The mechanical recoil slide in Time Crisis guns was engineered to mimic the tactile feel of a real firearm slide.
facts_and_myths.explanation: An internal heavy solenoid snaps the plastic slide backward with every shot, giving arcade players an authentic tactile feedback kick.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The game's strict time limit prevents players from hiding behind cover indefinitely.

facts_and_myths.claim: Enemy bullets in Time Crisis always hit you immediately with zero warning.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Standard white-clad enemy shots miss or graze cover; only enemies firing glowing red muzzle flashes or yelling voice alerts indicate a lethal incoming hit.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Releasing the foot pedal makes the player 100% invulnerable to all enemy bullet fire.

name: Skeeball
visual_anchor: Low-angle vertical shot looking up an inclined wooden bowling ramp, a heavy polished wooden ball launching off a curved ball-hop ramp into a 100-point bullseye cylinder.
core_traits: Classic arcade midway alley roller game played on an inclined wooden bowling runway
Players roll heavy composite balls up the ramp and off a curved launch lip (ball-hop)
Balls soar into a series of raised concentric circular rings with values from 10 to 100 points
Scores are redeemed for paper arcade tickets traded for prizes at the redemption counter

facts_and_myths.claim: Skeeball was patented in 1908, making it one of the oldest mechanical amusement games in history.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Inventor J. Dickinson Este patented Skee-Ball in Philadelphia in 1908, initially building thirty-two-foot alleys before shortening them to modern fourteen-foot lanes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The game is officially recognized as the very first redemption ticket sport in amusement parks.

facts_and_myths.claim: Throwing or lofting the ball through the air like a baseball pitch is allowed in tournament play.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Official rules mandate that the ball must be smoothly rolled along the wooden planks; chucking or bouncing overhand leads to disqualification.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tournament players aim exclusively for the 40-point and 50-point rings to achieve consistent high-average scores.

name: Whac-A-Mole
visual_anchor: Chaotic vertical perspective of five circular mole holes in an arcade cabinet, a soft black rubber mallet mid-swing slamming down on a pop-up grinning plastic mole.
core_traits: Popular mechanical arcade redemption game featuring a cabinet waist-high console with five holes
Mechanical plastic moles pop up randomly from holes driven by internal pneumatic or solenoids
Players swing a soft, lightweight rubber mallet to strike moles back into their holes before they retract
Speed of mole emergence accelerates as the timer runs down, awarding points and redemption tickets

facts_and_myths.claim: The term 'Whack-a-Mole' entered the English dictionary as a universal idiom for frustrating recurring problems.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The phrase is widely used in politics, cybersecurity, and business to describe situations where fixing one problem causes identical problems to pop up elsewhere.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Whac-A-Mole was originally invented in 1976 by Aaron Fechter and popularized commercially by Bob's Space Racers.

facts_and_myths.claim: Hitting the moles with bare fists or knees scores valid points and is endorsed by arcades.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The game is designed strictly for use with the supplied foam-rubber mallet; hitting with bare hands or feet risks damaging delicate mechanical sensors or injuring wrists.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The official commercial trademark omits the 'k', spelled 'Whac-A-Mole'.
